Experiment:
Heading: Overview and Objectives
Step 1: State the hypothesis and goals.
- Hypothesis: Oxygen post-annealing of LaMnO3−δ (LMO) buffer layers contracts the LMO pseudo-cubic lattice (≈3.92 Å → ≈3.85 Å) by reducing oxygen vacancies and oxidizing Mn3+ to Mn4+, thereby reducing lattice mismatch with YBa2Cu3O7−δ (YBCO; in-plane ≈3.85 Å). This reduces interfacial misfit strain and misfit dislocation density, suppresses a-axis oriented YBCO grains, enhances c-axis epitaxy, and improves critical current (Ic) by ~20% at 77 K self-field in second-generation coated conductors.
- Goals: (i) Quantify how LMO lattice parameter, texture, and surface topography evolve with O2 annealing; (ii) establish causal links among mismatch, defect density, a-axis grain fraction, and transport performance; (iii) demonstrate uniform enhancement on 1 m and 60 m tapes using roll-to-roll (R2R) processes.

Heading: Experimental Design
Step 2: Define architecture and fixed variables.
- Substrate architecture: Hastelloy C-276 (50–100 μm) with buffer stack Al2O3 (~10 nm)/Y2O3 (~100 nm)/IBAD-MgO (~10–12 nm)/epi-MgO (~30–50 nm)/LMO (50–150 nm).
- YBCO deposition: low-fluorine MOD, target thickness 1.2–1.5 μm across all samples; identical precursor chemistry, pyrolysis, and crystallization schedule for all experiments.
- Texture constraints: Maintain IBAD-MgO texture Δφ ~7–8°; epi-MgO Δφ ≤ 6°. Do not alter IBAD conditions during the study.
- Environmental constants during YBCO growth and oxygenation: identical gas composition and humidity; identical post-growth oxygenation to reach δ ≲ 0.1 in YBCO.

Step 3: Baseline and comparator groups.
- Baseline LMO (as-deposited): DC reactive sputtered LMO (oxygen-deficient, a_pc ≈ 3.90–3.92 Å), no post-anneal.
- Comparator A (oxygen-annealed LMO): Post-annealed in O2 (500–620 °C, 0–120 min, pO2 = 0.21–1 atm) to contract a_pc down to ≈3.85 Å.
- Comparator B (inert anneal control): Annealed in high-purity N2 at identical temperature/time cycles to rule out thermal-only effects (no oxygen uptake).
- Comparator C (over-anneal boundary): O2 anneal at upper bound (e.g., 620 °C, 120 min, 1 atm) to probe risk of over-oxidation, textural degradation, or interdiffusion.
- Thickness control: LMO thickness at 50 nm, 100 nm, 150 nm across selected anneal conditions to check thickness-dependent oxygenation and misfit relaxation.

Step 4: Experimental matrix (screening on coupons; then scale-up).
- Screening (coupon-level): 10 cm long, 12 mm wide sections across three spools; for each, prepare:
  • Temperatures: 500, 560, 590, 620 °C.
  • Dwell times: 0 (no anneal), 15, 30, 60, 120 min.
  • Atmospheres: Air (pO2 ≈ 0.21 atm) and O2 (1 atm); plus N2 (control).
  • Total unique conditions: 4 temps × 5 times × 2 O2 levels + N2 controls at 560 and 590 °C for 30 min = 40 + 2 = 42.
  • For 6 selected conditions (spanning a_pc ≈ 3.92 → 3.85 Å), add LMO thickness variation (50/100/150 nm) → 18 more.
- Scale-up (R2R): Select top 2–3 O2 anneal conditions (best Ic and microstructure) and run:
  • 1 m tapes (n = 3 per condition).
  • 60 m tape (n = 1 best condition) to assess uniformity and industrial viability.

Step 5: Sample processing sequence (to ensure comparability).
- Sequence fixed for all samples:
  1) IBAD-MgO/epi-MgO buffer completion (confirmed texture).
  2) LMO deposition by DC reactive sputtering (identical power, pressure, substrate temperature, and pO2 for the batch).
  3) Post-anneal of LMO under defined condition (only variable).
  4) YBCO low-fluorine MOD deposition under identical schedule.
  5) YBCO oxygenation to set δ.
  6) Contactless Ic mapping and four-probe validation on selected coupons.

Step 6: Ablation studies to test causal mechanisms.
- Composition tuning ablation: Compare O2-annealed vs N2-annealed LMO at same T, t → isolates oxygen chemistry from thermal effects on lattice parameter and texture.
- Interface tuning ablation: Keep LMO a_pc matched (≈3.85 Å) but introduce a thin interfacial Ca-doped CeO2 barrier (2–5 nm) on a subset to test whether reduced mismatch alone (without added interlayer) yields the same suppression of a-axis grains; if added barrier brings no further gain, mismatch reduction is the dominant mechanism. (Barrier layer optional and confined to small subset due to process complexity.)
- Texture tuning ablation: Mildly degrade LMO texture by intentionally lowering sputter substrate temperature by 50–70 °C during LMO growth (without O2 anneal), then apply the same O2 anneal to see whether restored lattice matching without good texture still suppresses a-axis grains. This separates texture from lattice parameter effects.
- Stress tuning ablation: Vary LMO thickness to modulate relaxation and residual strain; analyze sin2ψ XRD residual stress and relate to misfit dislocation spacing in cross-sectional TEM.
- Grain boundary tuning ablation: Correlate a-axis grain fraction from XRD with in-plane texture (Δφ) and Ic; intentionally promote a-axis growth by increasing YBCO crystallization heating rate by 20% in a small subset (control) to observe sensitivity of a-axis fraction to interface-mismatch condition.

Step 7: Characterization and metrics.
- LMO structure:
  • XRD θ–2θ scans for LMO (00l) peaks; extract a_pc from (001) peak near 2θ ≈ 23° (Cu Kα).
  • XRD rocking curve (ω) for LMO (00l): Δω target ≤ 2.5° (no deterioration with O2 anneal).
  • φ-scans of LMO (101) to quantify in-plane texture: Δφ target ≈ 7°.
  • Raman spectroscopy (500–650 cm−1): track Mn–O stretching modes; increased frequency and sharpening indicate shorter Mn–O bonds and reduced VO.
  • XPS (Mn 2p, Mn 3s) or XANES (optional) to quantify Mn3+/Mn4+ ratio; correlate with a_pc.
  • AFM (5 × 5 μm2): RMS roughness target ≤ 2 nm; verify no grain coarsening.
- Interface and defects:
  • Cross-sectional TEM on select samples: measure misfit dislocation spacing at LMO/YBCO; identify interfacial secondary phases; quantify thickness uniformity; measure a-axis lamellae, stacking faults.
  • XRD residual stress (sin2ψ) for LMO and YBCO; compare among anneal conditions.
- YBCO orientation and crystallinity:
  • XRD θ–2θ: quantify c-axis (00l) intensities; measure a-axis (h00) peak intensities; compute a-axis fraction Fa = ΣI(h00)/[ΣI(00l) + ΣI(h00)]. Target Fa ≤ 1–2%.
  • Rocking curve Δω(005) target ≤ 2.0°; φ-scan Δφ(103) target ≤ 7°.
- Superconducting properties:
  • Contactless Ic mapping at 77 K, self-field (magnetic induction method); calibrate with four-probe on short sections (1–5 cm) using 1 μV/cm criterion.
  • Jc(H, T) at 30–77 K and μ0H = 0–9 T; compute pinning force Fp = μ0 Jc H.
  • Tc and ρ(T) on small coupons to verify oxygenation (Tc ≈ 90 K).
- Uniformity:
  • Along-length mapping: every 5–10 m on the 60 m run, record a_pc (LMO) by XRD spot scans, texture (Δφ, Δω), surface RMS on selected locations, and Ic.

Step 8: Data analysis and evaluation criteria.
- Primary performance metric: Ic (77 K, self-field) per 12 mm width.
  • Success criterion: ≥ 20% improvement vs baseline as-deposited LMO; achieve ≥ 500 A/12 mm on 1 m tapes; demonstrate ≥ 560 A/12 mm peak and within ±5% along 60 m.
- Microstructural criteria:
  • LMO a_pc contraction to 3.85 ± 0.01 Å; Δφ ≈ 7° ± 1°; Δω ≤ 2.5°; RMS ≤ 2 nm.
  • YBCO c-axis quality: Δω(005) ≤ 2.0°; Δφ(103) ≤ 7.0°; a-axis fraction Fa ≤ 1–2%.
- Statistical treatment:
  • For screening, n ≥ 3 tapes per condition; analyze with ANOVA for Ic, Δω, Fa vs a_pc; post-hoc Tukey with α = 0.05.
  • Regression: Ic vs (lattice mismatch |f|), where f = (aLMO − aYBCO)/aYBCO. Expect monotonic improvement as |f| → 0. Fit linear or quadratic; report R2.
  • Mediation analysis: test whether reduction in Fa mediates the effect of a_pc on Ic.
- Mechanistic validation:
  • Show that O2-annealed (reduced VO, higher Mn4+) reduces a_pc and misfit dislocation density in TEM; N2-annealed samples do not replicate improvements.
  • Correlate Raman Mn–O stretching frequency shift with a_pc and Ic.
  • Demonstrate that texture (Δφ, Δω) is preserved through annealing (texture tuning objective met).

Heading: Implementation of Technologies/Methods
Step 9: LMO deposition by DC reactive magnetron sputtering.
- Target: Stoichiometric LaMnO3 ceramic; 2–3 inch for lab tool, larger for R2R.
- Conditions (typical, to be tuned for uniformity):
  • Power: 100–200 W DC; pressure: 3–5 mTorr; Ar/O2 = 90/10 to 95/5; substrate temperature: 500–600 °C to promote epitaxy on epi-MgO.
  • Film thickness: 100 nm baseline; deposition rate ≈ 0.5–1.0 nm/s.
  • Achieve as-deposited a_pc ≈ 3.90–3.92 Å (oxygen-deficient).
- Texture transfer: Ensure epitaxial cube-on-cube LMO//MgO; monitor in situ by RHEED if available (lab-scale) or ex situ XRD line scans (R2R).

Step 10: Oxygen post-annealing of LMO (composition tuning).
- Furnace/atmosphere:
  • For coupons: box furnace with high-purity O2 or air; flow 1–5 slm; ramp 10 °C/min.
  • For R2R: infrared or radiant heater zone in pure O2 (0.5–1 atm), residence times set by line speed and zone length.
- Parameters:
  • Screening: 500, 560, 590, 620 °C; dwell 0–120 min.
  • Atmosphere: O2 (1 atm) and air (0.21 atm); add N2 controls.
- Rationale (diffusion length): For D_O ~10^−10–10^−12 cm2/s at 500–600 °C in perovskites, 30–60 min suffices for 50–150 nm films (diffusion length ≫ film thickness).
- Expected signatures:
  • XRD peak shift to higher 2θ indicating lattice contraction toward ≈3.85 Å.
  • Raman Mn–O stretching mode hardening and narrowing.
  • XPS: increased Mn4+ spectral weight (e.g., Mn 3s multiplet splitting reduction).

Step 11: Interface and stress control (interface/stress tuning).
- Maintain epi-MgO and LMO surface smoothness (RMS ≤ 2 nm) to avoid step-induced a-axis nucleation.
- Optional ultrathin CeO2 cap (2–5 nm) only for interface ablation subset; standard process excludes cap to isolate LMO oxygenation effects.
- Residual stress measurement by XRD sin2ψ on LMO (00l) and YBCO (00l); reduced in-plane strain expected as mismatch |f| decreases.

Step 12: YBCO low-fluorine MOD process.
- Precursor solution: Low-F TFA-based with F:metal ratio ≲ 0.5; solution solids 0.5–1.0 M.
- Coating: Slot-die or dip-coating; target final thickness 1.2–1.5 μm via single or multiple coats with intermediate pyrolysis.
- Pyrolysis: 400–450 °C in flowing O2/N2 with 5–15% humidity to remove organics and fluorides, ramp 5–10 °C/min, dwell 30–60 min.
- Crystallization: 760–800 °C in O2 with controlled humidity (200–1000 ppm H2O), dwell 30–60 min; cool in O2 to 450 °C.
- Oxygenation: Hold at 400–450 °C in O2 for 1–2 h to achieve δ ≲ 0.1; confirm Tc ≈ 90 K on test coupons.
- Keep all YBCO steps identical across samples to isolate LMO effects.

Step 13: Texture and morphology control (texture tuning).
- Preserve IBAD-MgO and LMO biaxial texture: confirm Δφ and Δω after O2 anneal; avoid anneal conditions that induce recrystallization or grain coarsening.
- AFM screening: reject any LMO surface with RMS > 3 nm before YBCO deposition.

Step 14: Measurements and instrumentation.
- XRD: θ–2θ, ω rocking curves, φ scans; pole figures if available; spot size ~1–2 mm for along-length mapping.
- Raman: 532 nm excitation; acquire 450–750 cm−1; fit Mn–O stretching modes; monitor peak shift and FWHM.
- AFM: Tapping mode; 5 × 5 μm2 and 1 × 1 μm2 scans; extract RMS.
- XPS: Monochromatic Al Kα; Mn 2p, 3s regions; perform ion-milling carefully or angle-resolved to avoid damage; quantify Mn valence trends.
- TEM: FIB cross-sections on select best/worst; HAADF-STEM, GPA strain mapping, misfit dislocation densities at LMO/YBCO; measure a-axis lamellae density.
- Ic mapping: Contactless magnetic induction scanner; calibrate with four-probe on short sections. Use standard V–I criterion 1 μV/cm for four-probe; correct for self-field differences. For R2R, map Ic every 5–10 m.
- Jc(H, T): PPMS or 77 K variable-field setup; compute Fp = μ0 Jc H; compare Fp,max and scaling with reduced field.

Heading: Feasibility Assessment
Step 15: Resources and timeline.
- Equipment: Existing R2R DC sputter coater for LMO; R2R MOD line; tube/box furnaces with O2; XRD, AFM, Raman, XPS; access to TEM (shared facility); Ic mapping system; four-probe station; cryogenics (LN2, variable-T magnet).
- Personnel: 1 thin-film process engineer (LMO, anneal), 1 solution process engineer (MOD YBCO), 1 characterization scientist, 1 data analyst; shared TEM operator.
- Timeline:
  • Months 0–1: Process calibration (as-deposited LMO reproducibility, textural checks).
  • Months 1–3: Screening matrix on coupons; down-select best 2–3 anneal conditions.
  • Months 3–4: 1 m tapes for the top conditions; Ic and microstructure.
  • Months 4–6: 60 m demonstration for best condition; uniformity analysis and final validation.

Step 16: Risks and mitigation.
- Over-oxidation of LMO causing texture degradation or phase change.
  • Mitigation: Cap temperature ≤ 620 °C; monitor Δφ, Δω post-anneal; shorten dwell if texture worsens.
- Oxygen-induced oxidation of underlying metal.
  • Mitigation: Ensure integrity of Al2O3/Y2O3 barrier; inspect after anneal by XRD and TEM; limit O2 partial pressure to 0.21–1 atm and keep dwell minimal for full oxygenation of thin LMO.
- Mn interdiffusion into YBCO at high T.
  • Mitigation: Limit LMO anneal before YBCO deposition; avoid high-temperature (>800 °C) exposures with YBCO present; consider optional 2–5 nm CeO2 cap in ablation subset if interdiffusion is observed.
- Non-uniform oxygen uptake along length.
  • Mitigation: Uniform gas flow and line speed; real-time temperature profiling; along-length XRD spot checks.
- Measurement uncertainty in contactless Ic.
  • Mitigation: Routine calibration against four-probe on multiple segments; use consistent models (Bean strip) and geometry factors.

Heading: References to Previous Studies (pre-2025)
Step 17: Cite foundational and supporting literature.
- J. D. Jorgensen et al., Structural properties of oxygen-deficient YBa2Cu3O7−δ, Phys. Rev. B 41, 1863 (1990) — YBCO lattice and oxygenation.
- S. R. Foltyn et al., Materials science challenges for high-temperature superconducting wire, Nature Materials 6, 631–642 (2007) — Coated conductor overview, texture, Ic.
- P. N. Arendt et al., Rolling-assisted biaxially textured substrates and buffer layers for high-temperature superconductors, MRS Bulletin 29, 543–550 (2004) — IBAD templates and texture metrics.
- Y. Iijima et al., In-plane aligned YBa2Cu3O7−x thin films on polycrystalline metallic substrates, Appl. Phys. Lett. 60, 769 (1992) — Early IBAD-based coated conductor concepts.
- J. Töpfer and J. B. Goodenough, LaMnO3+δ Revisited, J. Solid State Chem. 130, 117–128 (1997) — Oxygen nonstoichiometry, Mn valence, lattice evolution in LaMnO3±δ.
- J. Mizusaki et al., Oxygen nonstoichiometry and defect structure of La1−xSrxMnO3−δ, Solid State Ionics 129, 163–177 (2000) — Oxygen transport and defect chemistry in perovskite manganites.
- M. N. Iliev et al., Raman spectroscopy of orthorhombic perovskite LaMnO3 and La1−xSrxMnO3, Phys. Rev. B 57, 2872 (1998) — Mn–O vibrational modes vs oxygen content/structure.
- J. W. Matthews and A. E. Blakeslee, Defects in epitaxial multilayers: I. Misfit dislocations, J. Cryst. Growth 27, 118–125 (1974) — Misfit dislocation and critical thickness framework.
- T. Haage et al., Growth mechanism and microstructure of a-axis oriented YBa2Cu3O7−δ thin films, Phys. Rev. B 56, 840–850 (1997) — Origins and suppression of a-axis grains.
- T. Izumi and Y. Shiohara, Development of coated conductors by the MOD method, Physica C 463–465, 510–515 (2007) — MOD/TFA process fundamentals.
- A. Xu et al., Low-fluorine solution growth of YBCO films for coated conductors, Supercond. Sci. Technol. 23, 014003 (2010) — Low-fluorine MOD chemistry and processing.
- E. H. Brandt and M. V. Indenbom, Type-II-superconductor strip with current in a perpendicular magnetic field, Phys. Rev. B 48, 12893 (1993) — Magnetization modeling relevant to contactless Ic.
- M. Oomen et al., An improved method to determine the critical current of HTS tapes by magnetic measurements, IEEE Trans. Appl. Supercond. 9, 1677–1680 (1999) — Inductive Ic measurement methodology.
- A. Goyal, Second-generation high temperature superconducting wires, MRS Bulletin 29, 552–561 (2004) — Texture transfer and coated conductor performance.
- J. H. Durrell et al., The behavior of coated conductors in magnetic fields, Supercond. Sci. Technol. 26, 093001 (2013) — Jc(H) and pinning in coated conductors.

Heading: Clarity Notes (key concepts explained)
Step 18: Explain critical concepts.
- Lattice mismatch f: The relative difference between in-plane lattice constants of film and underlying layer: f = (a_film − a_sub)/a_sub. Smaller |f| reduces misfit dislocations and interfacial strain.
- a-axis vs c-axis orientation: In YBCO, c-axis perpendicular to the substrate is desired for optimal current. a-axis grains (with a-axis out-of-plane) interrupt current paths and reduce Ic.
- Texture metrics: Δω (rocking curve FWHM) quantifies out-of-plane spread; Δφ (phi-scan FWHM) quantifies in-plane spread. Smaller values indicate better alignment.
- Oxygen vacancies (VO) in LMO: Missing oxygen increases Mn–O bond length and lattice parameter; oxygen annealing fills VO, oxidizes Mn3+ to Mn4+, shortens Mn–O bonds, and contracts the lattice.
- Inductive Ic measurement: A contactless magnetic method infers Ic from the field generated by shielding currents under an applied AC field, calibrated against transport standards.

Heading: Expected Outcomes and Decision Points
Step 19: Decision-making and scale-up.
- Select the O2 anneal condition achieving a_pc ≈ 3.85 Å, Δφ/Δω preserved, AFM RMS ≤ 2 nm, Fa ≤ 1–2%, and ≥ 20% Ic improvement vs baseline.
- If N2-annealed controls do not show improvement while O2-annealed do, oxygen chemistry is validated as the key mechanism.
- Proceed to 60 m R2R run with the best condition; accept if along-length Ic variation ≤ ±5% with peak ≥ 560 A/12 mm at 77 K self-field and microstructural metrics within targets.

[Experimental Workflow]
Step 1: Substrate preparation  
- Start with 50 µm-thick, 12 mm-wide Hastelloy C-276 tapes.  
- Electrochemically polish and clean the tapes.

Step 2: Multilayer buffer deposition (roll-to-roll, SCSC)  
- Deposit sequentially by industrial roll-to-roll systems:  
  – Al₂O₃ (60 nm) barrier layer  
  – Y₂O₃ (10 nm) nucleation seed layer  
  – IBAD-MgO (10 nm) biaxial-texture layer  
  – Epi-MgO (60 nm) texture-repair layer  

Step 3: LMO buffer deposition  
- Deposit 50 nm LaMnO₃−δ film by DC reactive magnetron sputtering in roll-to-roll mode.  
  – Target: 99.95 % pure La:Mn (1:1 atomic ratio) alloy.  
  – Gas: Ar/O₂ mixture, total pressure 1 Pa; Ar 135 sccm, O₂ 20–25 sccm.  
  – Power: 1000 W; substrate temperature 750 °C (induction heating).

Step 4: Post-annealing of LMO films  
- Anneal LMO-coated short samples (temperature series: 500 °C – 620 °C in 20 °C steps; time series at 550 °C: 5 min – 2 h).  
- Atmosphere: flowing 99.999 % O₂, slight over-pressure ≈ 1.05 atm.  
- Heating rate: 5 °C min⁻¹; cool naturally to room temperature.

Step 5: LMO characterization  
- XRD θ–2θ scans (Cu Kα, 20–55°) to track (00ℓ) peak shifts and extract lattice constant.

Step 6: YBCO deposition  
- Deposit 1.5 µm YBCO film on each LMO template by low-fluorine metal–organic deposition (MOD) in the same roll-to-roll line (SCSC); processing details referenced but not repeated in the paper.

Step 7: YBCO characterization  
- XRD θ–2θ, ω, φ scans to check c-axis orientation and texture.  
- Measure critical current Ic at 77 K, self-field with dynamic contact-free Mcorder system (magnetic induction).  
- For selected samples, measure field-dependent Ic and pinning force density Fp at 30 K, 50 K, 77 K (magnetic field range not specified in the paper).

Experiment:
Step1: Objectives and Hypotheses
- Objective: Quantitatively validate that a layered precursor strategy (C-MPP), which stacks a conventional Y123+Y211 (CPP) top layer over an in-situ MPP layer (Y2O3 + Ba–Cu–O), produces single-domain YBa2Cu3O7−δ bulks with finer, more homogeneous Y211 nanoparticle dispersion, lower porosity and zero macro-cracks, resulting in higher force–volume density and lower magnetic relaxation at 77 K, without degrading epitaxial texture or mechanical robustness required for HTS Maglev service.
- Hypotheses:
  1) The C-MPP architecture increases the Y211/Y123 interfacial area via capillary-driven solute infiltration from the MPP layer into the CPP layer during TSMG, enhancing flux pinning and reducing magnetic relaxation rate R compared to CPP and MPP baselines.
  2) A CPP buffer pellet beneath a SmBCO seed mitigates seed corrosion by Ba–Cu–O liquid and maintains single-domain epitaxy with a-b plane texture comparable to CPP.
  3) C-MPP reduces oxygen porosity and eliminates macro-cracks relative to MPP by lowering internal gas pressure and balancing shrinkage, yielding higher levitation stiffness and force–volume density at 77 K.

Step2: Experimental Design (Baseline, Comparisons, Ablations, Evaluation Criteria)
- Experimental groups (all with 1 wt% CeO2 and Yb2O3 substrate barrier unless noted):
  G1 (CPP baseline): Single-layer CPP pellet (Y123 + 35 mol% Y211).
  G2 (MPP baseline): Single-layer MPP pellet (Y2O3 + Ba2Cu3Ox to form Y211 in situ) with identical geometry.
  G3 (C-MPP target): Two-layer pellet: top CPP (Y123 + 35 mol% Y211), bottom MPP (Y2O3 + Ba2Cu3Ox), with a 6 mm-diameter CPP buffer pellet under SmBCO seed.
  Ablations to deconvolve mechanisms:
  A1 (No-buffer): Same as G3 but remove the 6 mm CPP buffer pellet to test seed corrosion/texture robustness.
  A2 (No-CeO2): Same as G3 but without CeO2 to test Y211 coarsening suppression.
  A3 (No-Yb2O3 barrier): Same as G3 but remove the Yb2O3 substrate layer to quantify stray grain formation impact.
  A4 (Reverse-stack): MPP on top, CPP bottom, to test directionality of solute infiltration on Y211 distribution and texture.
  A5 (Layer-thickness scan): G3 with top:bottom thickness ratios of 30:70, 45:55, 60:40 to identify optimal architecture.
- Sample geometry and batch: Discs of 25.0 ± 0.2 mm diameter, 9.5 ± 0.1 mm thickness (a-b area ≈ 491 mm²), N = 7 per group for statistical power (minimum 5 usable per group after yield).
- Thermal history control: Process all groups per batch in the same furnace run and identical thermal schedule; arrange pellets symmetrically around the furnace hot zone to equalize thermal gradients. Use identical oxygenation protocol.
- Primary endpoints:
  1) Levitation performance at 77 K in LN2: force–volume density Fv (N mm−3) and stiffness (dF/dz) above a Halbach guideway; relaxation rate R over 180 s.
  2) Microstructure: Porosity (%) by image analysis in a–c sections; presence/size of macro-cracks; Y211 particle size distribution and spatial homogeneity; epitaxial texture quality.
- Secondary endpoints:
  1) Trapped field (field-cooled, 77 K) and magnetization-derived Jc (Bean model).
  2) Mechanical integrity: Vickers hardness and indentation fracture toughness; 3-point flexural strength; cyclic magnetic loading durability.
- Statistical analysis:
  - One-way ANOVA with Tukey HSD for group comparisons of Fv, R, porosity, crack metrics, stiffness, Jc.
  - Regression/correlation between microstructural metrics (Y211 size, porosity) and performance (R, Fv).
  - Effect sizes (Cohen’s d) and 95% confidence intervals.
- Outcome criteria aligned to Maglev targets:
  - Fv improvement ≥ 5% vs CPP baseline with equal or lower R.
  - Porosity ≤ 18% and no macro-cracks > 100 μm in a–c cross-sections.
  - Epitaxial texture: in-plane alignment comparable to CPP (e.g., (103) XRD φ-scan FWHM within ±10% of CPP; rocking-curve Δω < ~3° typical for single-domain bulks).
  - No parasitic grains observed in optical/SEM over full cross-section.

Step3: Materials and Powder Preparation
- Powders and additives:
  - CPP powder: YBa2Cu3O7−δ (Y123) + 35 mol% Y2BaCuO5 (Y211), plus 1 wt% CeO2 (relative to total mass). Grain size target: Y123 d50 ~1–3 μm; Y211 0.5–2 μm (starting), refined by CeO2 during melt processing.
  - MPP powder: Y2O3 and Ba2Cu3Ox (liquid source). Mix molar ratio to yield stoichiometric formation of Y211 plus Ba–Cu–O liquid; practical mixture: Y2O3:(BaCuO2 + CuO) chosen to achieve a Ba:Cu ≈ 2:3 to form Ba2Cu3Ox liquid near 1010–1030 °C; include 1 wt% CeO2.
  - Substrate barrier: Yb2O3 powder layer (~0.3 mm thick) on Al2O3 setter to suppress stray nucleation.
  - Binder: 2 wt% polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) aqueous solution for green strength; burnout accommodated in thermal schedule.
- Mixing:
  - Wet ball-mill each powder composition separately in isopropanol with 0.5 wt% dispersant (e.g., fish oil or commercial dispersant) for 8 h at 300 rpm using ZrO2 media; dry at 80 °C; sieve through 200 mesh.
- Granulation and pressing:
  - Add 2 wt% PVA, granulate, dry; uniaxial press top and bottom layers separately.
  - Main pellet assembly: For G3 baseline, top CPP layer 4.0 mm thickness, bottom MPP layer 5.5 mm thickness (also vary per A5). Diameter 25 mm.
  - Cold isostatic pressing (CIP) 150 MPa to consolidate the stacked pellet.
- Seed and buffer:
  - SmBCO single-crystal seed (e.g., SmBa2Cu3O7-based) oriented with a-b plane parallel to pellet top surface; four-facet lines expected post-growth.
  - 6 mm-diameter, 2–3 mm-thick CPP buffer pellet (same CPP composition) directly under the seed for G3; omitted in A1.
- Assembly:
  - Place Yb2O3 powder layer (0.3 mm) on dense Al2O3 setter; center the pellet; lightly dust pellet perimeter with Y2O3 to minimize sticking. Fix the seed and buffer by slight indentation in the top surface.

Step4: Top-Seeded Melt-Growth (TSMG) Thermal Schedule
- Furnace: Vertical high-temperature box furnace with Pt–Rh thermocouple near sample; temperature uniformity ±2 °C over 60 mm zone.
- Schedule (typical for YBCO; ensure seed safety by staying below SmBCO peritectic ~1060–1080 °C):
  1) Binder burnout: Ramp 1 °C/min to 500 °C, hold 2 h in flowing O2/air mix (50:50), then to 700 °C at 1 °C/min, hold 1 h.
  2) Melt step: Ramp 2 °C/min to 1035 °C, hold 1 h (above Y123 peritectic but below SmBCO seed decomposition) to form Ba–Cu–O liquid and Y211 solid.
  3) Controlled slow cool for textured growth: Cool 0.5 °C/min to 1000 °C; then 0.3 °C/min to 980 °C; then 0.2 °C/min to 950 °C to promote steady growth front and minimize thermal stress.
  4) Furnace cool to 500 °C at 1 °C/min; then to room temperature.
- Notes:
  - Identical schedule for all groups in the same run to isolate composition/architecture effects.
  - Hold/ramps may be adjusted by ±5 °C based on preliminary melt-wet tests; maintain seed integrity (inspect post-run).

Step5: Oxygenation Protocol
- Goal: Achieve δ ≈ 0.07 (YBa2Cu3O6.93) for optimal Tc and intergranular connectivity while minimizing oxygenation cracking.
- Schedule:
  1) Ramp at 20 °C/h to 450 °C in flowing O2 (1 bar), hold 220 h (consistent with thick bulk oxygen diffusion times).
  2) Slow cool to 300 °C at 10 °C/h; then to room temperature at 20 °C/h.
- Monitoring: Weight change before/after oxygenation; optional microhardness checks indicative of oxygen content.

Step6: Microstructure and Texture Characterization
- Density and porosity:
  - Polished a–c cross-sections (diamond suspensions down to 1 μm); optical microscopy to capture ≥10 fields per sample at fixed magnification; ImageJ threshold-based segmentation with calibration to compute area porosity; report mean ± SD.
  - Archimedes density (ethanol) for bulk density cross-check.
- Y211 nanoparticles and distribution:
  - SEM/BSE imaging for Y211 dispersion mapping; EDS spot checks to identify Y211 vs Y123.
  - TEM on FIB-liftout lamellae near center and near the layer interface for particle size distribution (n ≥ 200 particles per region); quantify 20–260 nm target range; log-normal fits to d50.
- Macro-cracks and defects:
  - Low-mag optical survey of full cross-section; measure maximum crack opening and length; classify macro-cracks as >100 μm opening.
- Epitaxial texture:
  - XRD θ–2θ to confirm Y123 phase; pole figure or φ-scan of (103)/(102) to evaluate in-plane texture; rocking-curve Δω of (005) for c-axis alignment; compare to CPP baseline.
  - Optional EBSD (if surface prep permits) for grain orientation map over mm-scale region to confirm single-domain nature and absence of parasitic grains.

Step7: Magnetic and Electromagnetic Performance
- Levitation force and stiffness at 77 K:
  - Setup: SCML-type platform with a fixed Halbach NdFeB guideway providing 0.67 T at 5 mm above the track centerline; 6-axis stage controls gap (z) with 10 μm precision; force sensor resolution ≤0.1 N.
  - Zero-field-cooled (ZFC) loop: Cool bulk in LN2 well above guideway (>100 mm), approach at 0.5 mm/s to a minimum gap of 3 mm, record force vs gap during approach and retraction. Extract maximum levitation force Fmax and stiffness k = dF/dz at an operational gap (e.g., 5 mm).
  - 3-min relaxation: Hold at fixed gap (e.g., 5 mm) after reaching peak force; record force decay for 180 s; compute relaxation rate R = [F(0) − F(180 s)]/F(0) × 100%.
  - Normalization: Convert F to force–volume density Fv (N mm−3) by dividing by measured bulk volume; further normalize to a standard footprint and thickness using COMSOL multiphysics modeling (Step9) to ensure fair comparison across 441–676 mm² and 9–10 mm geometries.
- Magnetization and trapped field:
  - VSM or SQUID magnetometry on cores/mini-samples cut from rim (to avoid seed region) at 77 K and 65 K; compute Jc via Bean model from M–H loops.
  - Trapped field: Field-cool under 0.5 T axial field from an electromagnet, hold at 77 K for 5 min, switch-off field; map trapped field 1 mm above surface with a Hall probe over a 9×9 grid (spacing 2.5 mm). Report Btrap,max and field uniformity.

Step8: Mechanical Integrity and Durability
- Hardness and fracture toughness:
  - Vickers hardness HV at 1 kgf load (10 s dwell), 10 indents per sample; indentation fracture toughness KIC using semi-empirical models from radial crack lengths (report model used).
- Flexural strength:
  - 3-point bending on bars cut from outer ring (if sample volume allows) at room temperature and at 77 K (cryogenic fixture), span-to-depth ratio ~20, crosshead rate 0.5 mm/min.
- Cyclic magnetic loading durability:
  - Repeated ZFC approach–retract cycles between 3–9 mm gap at 2 Hz for 10,000 cycles at 77 K; monitor drift in peak force and stiffness every 100 cycles; post-test microstructure check for new cracks.

Step9: Numerical Modeling and Force Normalization (COMSOL H-Formulation)
- Purpose: Normalize levitation performance across small variations in sample area and thickness; interpret the effect of microstructure via Jc models.
- Model:
  - 3D H-formulation finite-element model of a superconducting bulk (25 mm disc, thickness 9–10 mm) above a Halbach PMG; magnet assembly modeled with remanent flux density Br = 1.3 T for NdFeB blocks arranged to yield 0.67 T at 5 mm gap. Surrounding air domain extends ≥5× sample size.
  - Superconductor constitutive law: E–J power law E = Ec (J/Jc)^n with Ec = 1 μV cm−1, n = 20; Jc(B) described by Kim-type model Jc(B) = Jc0 / (1 + |B|/B0) with anisotropy factor for c-axis vs a-b plane if needed; parameters calibrated to match measured M–H loops of CPP baseline.
  - Boundary conditions: Magnetic insulation at outer air boundaries; quasi-static approach simulated by sweeping gap in steps.
- Outputs:
  - Force vs gap curves for reference geometries to determine linear scaling coefficients within 9–10 mm thickness and 441–676 mm² area ranges.
  - Sensitivity analysis to Jc0 and B0 to relate microstructural changes (Y211 distribution) to performance changes.

Step10: Data Analysis and Interpretation
- Compare G3 (C-MPP) vs G1 (CPP) and G2 (MPP) on Fv, R, stiffness, porosity, Y211 size, crack metrics, texture. Use ANOVA/Tukey; report p-values and confidence intervals.
- Ablations:
  - A1 quantifies the role of buffer pellet on seed integrity and texture (expect increased seed corrosion, parasitic grains, degraded texture metrics if buffer is absent).
  - A2 isolates CeO2 action on Y211 coarsening (expect larger Y211, reduced Jc and higher R).
  - A3 tests the Yb2O3 barrier (expect stray grains at substrate interface and degraded single-domain integrity if absent).
  - A4 reveals directionality of solute infiltration (expect poorer Y211 enrichment in top region when reversed).
  - A5 yields optimum layer ratio by balancing infiltration and top-layer buffer function; fit quadratic response of Fv and R vs top-layer fraction.
- Correlate microstructure to performance:
  - Regression of R and Fv vs porosity, Y211 d50, and particle density; seek negative correlation of R with Y211 density and porosity.
- Acceptance conclusion if C-MPP meets or exceeds targets: ≥5% increase in Fv over CPP, R ≤ CPP, porosity ≤18%, no macro-cracks, texture equal to CPP.

Step11: Feasibility, Resources, and Timeline
- Equipment:
  - High-temperature box furnace with programmable controller; oxygenation furnace; precision presses (uniaxial + CIP); SEM/EDS, TEM access; XRD; force measurement stage with Halbach guideway; COMSOL Multiphysics license.
- Materials:
  - High-purity Y2O3, BaCO3, CuO precursors for Ba–Cu–O; commercially available Y123 and Y211 powders (or synthesized in-house); CeO2 nanopowder; SmBCO seeds; Yb2O3 powder; PVA binder.
- Personnel:
  - 1 senior researcher (process + design), 1 postdoc (characterization + modeling), 1 technician (furnace and machining).
- Timeline (approximate for N ≈ 40–50 bulks):
  - Month 1: Powder synthesis/qualification; pilot runs to validate schedule.
  - Months 2–3: Batch fabrication of all groups; oxygenation.
  - Month 4: Microstructure and texture characterization; levitation and magnetization testing.
  - Month 5: Mechanical tests; cyclic durability; TEM on selected samples.
  - Month 6: COMSOL modeling, data analysis, and reporting.
- Risks and mitigations:
  - Seed corrosion: Use CPP buffer pellet; keep melt peak ≤1035 °C; verify seed post-run.
  - Oxygenation cracks: Slow ramps and long holds; consider stepped oxygen partial pressure if needed.
  - Variability in infiltration: Tight control of green density and layer thickness; consistent powder PSD and binder content.
  - Yield loss due to handling: Use soft fixtures and compliant supports during processing.

Step12: Safety and Quality Control
- Safety: LN2 handling protocols; furnace hot-work procedures; powder inhalation precautions (respirators); cutting and polishing PPE.
- QC checkpoints:
  - Pre-run pellet mass/size; post-run dimensional shrinkage; seed alignment check.
  - Oxygen content proxy: measure Tc via AC susceptibility on small cores (expect Tc ~ 90–92 K if well-oxygenated).
  - Reproducibility: Duplicate runs for at least one group to confirm batch effects are negligible.

Step13: References to Previous Studies (pre-2025)
- D. A. Cardwell, “Processing and properties of large single grain (RE)–Ba–Cu–O superconductors,” Superconductor Science and Technology 15 (2002) R1–R16.
- Y. Shi and D. A. Cardwell, “Processing of bulk Y–Ba–Cu–O superconductors using the infiltration and growth technique,” Journal of the American Ceramic Society 89 (2006) 2038–2044.
- M. Tomita and M. Murakami, “High trapped fields in bulk Gd–Ba–Cu–O superconductors fabricated by melt processing,” Nature 421 (2003) 517–520.
- E. Pardo, “Modeling of trapped fields and magnetization in bulk superconductors using the H-formulation,” Superconductor Science and Technology 26 (2013) 105017.
- R. Brambilla, F. Grilli, and L. Martini, “Development of an edge-element model for AC loss computation in high-temperature superconductors using the H-formulation,” Superconductor Science and Technology 20 (2007) 16–24.
- J. R. Hull, “Superconducting magnetic levitation,” IEEE Transactions on Applied Superconductivity 7 (1997) 754–760.

Step14: Implementation Notes on Key Concepts
- Capillary-driven solute infiltration: During the melt step, Ba–Cu–O liquid formed in the MPP layer wicks into the porous network of the upper CPP via capillary forces, carrying dissolved rare-earth species and promoting in-situ precipitation of fine Y211 nanoparticles. This increases pinning center density without disrupting the a-b epitaxial framework established by the seed (cf. infiltration and growth literature).
- Role of CeO2: CeO2 reacts to form BaCeO3 nanoparticles that serve as heterogeneous nucleation sites and limit Ostwald ripening of Y211, maintaining a fine Y211 dispersion that elevates Jc at 77 K.
- Seed protection by CPP buffer: The CPP buffer physically separates the reactive Ba–Cu–O liquid from the SmBCO seed, reduces corrosive attack, and maintains a stable, reproducible epitaxial nucleation front.
- Yb2O3 substrate barrier: A refractory rare-earth oxide powder bed increases the heterogeneous nucleation barrier at the pellet–setter interface, suppressing stray grains and helping ensure single-domain growth.

[Experimental Workflow]
Step 1 – Precursor powder synthesis  
- Starting oxides: Y₂O₃, BaCO₃, CuO.  
- Three stoichiometric mixtures prepared:  
  – Y123 (YBa₂Cu₃O₇−δ)  
  – Y211 (Y₂BaCuO₅)  
  – Y023 (Ba₂Cu₃Oₓ)  
- Each mixture calcined twice (40 h per calcination) at 930 °C (Y123), 950 °C (Y211) and 880 °C (Y023).

Step 2 – Precursor powder blending  
- CPP: 35 mol % Y211 + balance Y123 + 1 wt % CeO₂.  
- MPP: 72.34 mol % Y₂O₃ (Y200) + Y023 + 1 wt % CeO₂.  
- Blending performed by ball-milling; no further milling parameters given.

Step 3 – Green-body preparation  
- 40 g powder pressed into 30 mm × 30 mm square pellets (thickness not specified).  
- C-MPP pellet: 20 g CPP powder placed above 20 g MPP powder in the same die and co-pressed.  
- Identical uniaxial pressing conditions used for all pellets (pressure value not specified).

Step 4 – Seed/buffer/substrate assembly (same for all pellets)  
- Top surface: one polished SmBCO single-crystal seed (a–b plane down).  
- Buffer mini-pellet (6 mm Ø × 2 mm thick, made from CPP) inserted between seed and main pellet.  
- Bottom layer: substrate of Y123 + Yb₂O₃ powders (functions as extra liquid source and nucleation barrier).  
- Entire assembly placed in furnace as illustrated in Fig. 1.

Step 5 – Top-seeded melt-growth (TSMG) heat treatment (all samples processed together)  
- Ramp to T_max = 1050 °C in 12 h; dwell 1.5 h.  
- Cool to T_s = 1010 °C at 80 °C h⁻¹ to initiate epitaxial growth.  
- Undercooling: 120 h linear cool to T_e = 970 °C.  
- Furnace cool to room temperature.  
- Seed, buffer and substrate mechanically removed afterwards.

Step 6 – Oxygenation  
- Samples annealed at 450 °C in flowing O₂ for 220 h.

Step 7 – Dimensional inspection and cutting  
- Samples measured (callipers) to obtain a–b plane area and c-axis thickness (Table 2).  
- Each bulk cut along the c-axis through the centre with a precision diamond wire saw.  
- Cut surface ground and polished with a precision diamond surface grinder/polisher.

Step 8 – Optical microstructure characterisation  
- Polished a–c cross-sections imaged with an optical microscope.  
- Three to four local regions (positions 1–3/4) selected for porosity quantification.  
- ImageJ software used to count pores (n) and measure average pore diameter (D).  
- Porosity calculated as (n × D)/S, where S is the inspected area (~2.71 mm²).

Step 9 – Levitation-force measurement  
- Instrument: custom-built SCML-05 platform (Fig. 3).  
- Magnet: second track of a Halbach NdFeB guideway; surface field 0.67 T at working height (WH) 5 mm.  
- Temperature: 77 K by continuous liquid-nitrogen cooling.  
- Two magnetisation modes:  
  – Zero-field cooling (ZFC): sample cooled at 60 mm above track, then lowered to 5 mm.  
  – Field cooling (FC): sample cooled at 30 mm above track, then lowered to 5 mm.  
- Procedure (identical for ZFC and FC):  
  1. Cool to 77 K at fixed height (ZFCH or FCH).  
  2. Lower to WH = 5 mm and immediately retract at 1 mm s⁻¹ to record force loop.  
  3. Lower again at 1 mm s⁻¹, hold 3 min to record force-relaxation curve.  
- Force data sampled continuously; maximum force (F_max) and minimum force after 3 min (F_min) extracted.  
- Relaxation rate R = (F_max – F_min)/F_max.

Step 10 – Finite-element (FE) normalisation of levitation force  
- COMSOL Multiphysics used with H-formulation.  
- PMG field first calculated analytically and imported (Fig. 12a).  
- 3-D bulk model created (Fig. 12b); J_c set to 1.1 × 10⁴ A cm⁻² (Bean model).  
- Parametric sweep: thickness h = 2–20 mm (step 0.1 mm between 9–10 mm) with fixed 26 mm × 26 mm a–b plane; then area S varied 441–676 mm² with h = 9.5 mm.  
- Linear regression performed on F_max and F_min vs. h (9–10 mm) and vs. S (441–676 mm²); slopes and R² recorded (Figs. 13–14).  
- Experimental forces normalised to a “standard” bulk of h = 9.5 mm and S = 550 mm² using the combined thickness-and-area coefficient k_v (Table 5).  
- Engineering densities calculated:  
  – Force-area density F_s = F_min/S  
  – Force-volume density F_v = F_min/V (Table 6).

[Experimental Design Details]
- All growth runs performed simultaneously in one furnace to ensure identical thermal history; a second C-MPP sample (CM3) processed in a different furnace for reproducibility check.  
- Temperature uniformity inside the furnace verified by multipoint thermocouples (details not given).  
- No porosity measurement uncertainty or image-analysis threshold specified.  
- Error bars or statistical spread of force values not provided.  
- Sample identification: CPP, MPP, CM1, CM2, CM3 (CM = C-MPP).

Experiment: Synergistic optimization of (Y,Nd,Sm,Gd)Ba2Cu3O7−x bulk hollow cylinders with RE-211 and WO3 nano-inclusions grown by seeded infiltration growth

— Overview and Objectives —
Step1: State the goal
- Objective: Rigorously validate and optimize a monolithic, net-shape hollow cylinder of (Y,NSG)BCO (Y0.8(Nd0.33Sm0.33Gd0.33)0.2Ba2Cu3O7−x) containing uniformly embedded micron RE-211 precipitates and 0.5 wt% WO3 nanoparticles processed by rapid-prototyped gelcasting (RPGC) and seeded infiltration growth (IG). Quantify how five levers—composition, interface, texture, stress (via Ba-excess), and grain-boundary elimination—synergize to maximize high-field Jc and magnetic shielding at 77 K.
- Target metrics to confirm: Jc(77 K, 0 T) ~4 kA cm−2; Jc(77 K, 8.5 T) ~0.4 kA cm−2; Fp,max(77 K) ~40 N cm−3 with peak field Bp ≈ 7–8 T; emergence of a secondary low-field Fp peak; single-grain (103) texture; sharp superconducting transition ΔTc ≤ 1.5 K; robust shielding ≥ 40 G at 77 K.

— Experimental Design (Baselines, Comparisons, Ablations, Analysis) —
Step2: Define sample matrix, baselines, and ablations
- Base control (B0): YBa2Cu3O7−x (Y-123) cylinder processed by conventional solid-state route + standard melt growth without IG and without seed; no WO3; standard Ba-Cu-O.
- Process control (B1): Y-123 cylinder via IG without seed and without WO3, Ba-stoichiometric infiltrant.
- Composition control (C0): (Y,NSG)BCO (20% RE mix) bars/cylinders by IG, no WO3, seeded.
- Interface control (I0): Y-123 + 0.5 wt% WO3, seeded IG, no RE substitution (Y only), same RE-211 fraction.
- Texture control (T0): (Y,NSG)BCO + WO3, IG without seed (random grain orientation).
- Stress/Ba control (S0): (Y,NSG)BCO + WO3, IG with seed but stoichiometric Ba (no 2 wt% Ba-excess).
- Full synergy (F): (Y,NSG)BCO + 0.5 wt% WO3, 30–40 vol% RE-211, excess Ba (2 wt% in infiltrant), seeded IG to impose single-grain (103) texture.
- Factor sweeps (for optimization and robustness):
  - RE substitution fraction: 0, 10, 20, 30 wt% of Y replaced by equimolar Nd/Sm/Gd on the Y site.
  - WO3 level: 0, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0 wt% (nominal, added to the ceramic solids).
  - RE-211 volume fraction: nominal 25, 35, 45 vol% (kept near 0.5–2 µm after heat treatment).
  - Cooling rate across growth window: 0.2, 0.5, 1.0 °C h−1.
  - Ba-excess in infiltrant: 0, 1, 2, 3 wt%.
- Replicates: n ≥ 3 per condition for bars; n ≥ 2 per condition for cylinders, to quantify variability.

Step3: Sample geometries and dimensions
- Hollow cylinders: OD 18–22 mm, ID 10–12 mm, height 20–25 mm, wall ~4–6 mm (compatible with shielding tests).
- Characterization bars: 2×2×10 mm3 bars cut from cylinder walls for VSM tests to avoid demagnetization complexities; retain annular rings (outer segment) for ring magnetization tests.

Step4: Measurement plan and evaluation criteria
- Structural: Powder XRD with Rietveld refinement; confirm orthorhombic a ≈ 3.82–3.89 Å, b ≈ 3.86–3.90 Å, c ≈ 11.67–11.75 Å, low impurity content (<5 wt% unwanted phases). Texture: XRD pole figures for (103), (001), (110); orientation spread FWHM ≤ 5–10° for single-grain.
- Microstructure: FE-SEM for RE-211 size distribution (target 0–2 µm modes); EDS maps of RE/Ba/Cu/W; TEM/HRTEM in selected samples to confirm stacking faults, WO3/BaWO4 nanoscale inclusions (2–10 nm) and their spacing.
- Superconductivity: AC susceptibility for Tc and ΔTc; four-probe resistivity for Tc,onset; oxygen stoichiometry inferred by Tc and lattice parameters.
- Magnetization: VSM M(H) loops up to 9 T at 10, 30, 50, 65, 77 K; extract Jc via extended Bean model (geometry-corrected for bars/rings). Define Fp = μ0 Jc H. Determine Fp(h) scaling; identify peak positions and exponents; estimate Hirr(T) by Kramer extrapolation.
- Shielding: DC shielding coefficient S = Bext/Bin versus applied field up to 50–100 G at 77 K; measure trapped field by field-cooling and flux mapping with Hall probe.
- Acceptance criteria for “synergy”: Full condition (F) must exceed all ablations in at least two metrics: Jc(77 K, 0 T) ≥ 4 kA cm−2; Jc(77 K, 8.5 T) ≥ 0.35–0.45 kA cm−2; Fp,max(77 K) ≥ 35 N cm−3; Bp near 7–8 T at 10–77 K; ΔTc ≤ 1.5–2 K; texture confirmed single grain.

Step5: Data analysis and statistics
- Use ANOVA across the factorial design to quantify main effects and interaction terms (composition × interface × texture × Ba-excess). Post-hoc Tukey test (α = 0.05).
- Pinning analysis: Normalize Fp by Fp,max and plot vs reduced field h = H/Hirr; fit to Dew-Hughes forms to distinguish δκ (mean free path/κ fluctuations) versus surface/point pinning; correlate secondary low-field peaks with nano-inclusion density and 211 interfaces.
- Reproducibility: Report means ± standard deviation; effect sizes (Cohen’s d) for improvements over baselines.

— Implementation of Technologies/Methods —
Step6: Powder/precursor synthesis
- RE-211 precursor: Prepare (Y0.8(Nd0.33Sm0.33Gd0.33)0.2)2BaCuO5 by solid-state reaction. Stoichiometric rare-earth oxides (Y2O3, Nd2O3, Sm2O3, Gd2O3, ≥99.9%), BaCO3, CuO powders. Ball-mill (isopropanol, 300 rpm, 24 h) with zirconia media. Calcine: 900 °C (12 h), re-mill, 950 °C (12 h), re-mill, 1000 °C (12 h). Confirm phase by XRD. Target median size d50 ~0.8–1.5 µm after milling/sieving.
- Infiltrant: Ba–Cu–O source as BaCuO2 + CuO mixture near eutectic (~Ba:Cu ≈ 1:1.2 molar) with 2 wt% Ba-excess option to generate Ba-rich liquid. Calcine 800–850 °C to form BaCuO2; verify by XRD.
- WO3 nanoparticles: Use commercial aqueous colloid or sol-gel-derived particles with 2–6 nm mean size, stabilized with citrate or polyacrylate dispersant. Prepare concentrated stock; verify hydrodynamic size by DLS prior to mixing.
- Oxygenation: High-purity O2 (≥99.999%) and flowing air supplies for heat treatments.

Step7: Sol-casting slurry and dispersion (for RPGC)
- Solids loading: 50–60 vol% mixture of RE-211 precursor powder with a minor seed fraction of preformed (Y,RE)-123 nuclei (~5–10 wt% of total solids) to assist initial reaction. Incorporate WO3 nanoparticles at target wt% relative to total ceramic solids.
- Dispersant: Ammonium polyacrylate (1–2 wt% of solids) in deionized water, adjust pH 8.5–9.5 with NH4OH for electrosteric stabilization.
- Gelcasting system: Acrylamide monomer (10–15 wt% of solution) and N,N′-methylenebisacrylamide crosslinker (1–3 mol% of monomer), initiated by ammonium persulfate (APS) with TEMED. Mix under inert atmosphere at 5–10 °C to retard premature gelation. Vacuum de-gas (−0.08 MPa, 5 min).
- Uniformity: Add WO3 colloid slowly under ultrasonication (100 W, 5–10 min) and high-shear mixing (2000–3000 rpm, 10 min). Confirm absence of nanoparticle agglomerates by dynamic light scattering on supernatant and by small-angle light scattering (optional).

Step8: Net-shape green body via rapid-prototyped molds
- 3D printed molds (stereolithography or SLA resin with release coating) defining OD/ID/height; include draft angles for demolding. Apply mold release (PTFE-based).
- Casting: Fill molds; vibrate gently (50–60 Hz, 2 min) to collapse trapped bubbles. In-situ gelation at 25–30 °C for 30–60 min. Demold after gel strength >0.5 MPa (finger test).
- Drying: Controlled humidity (50% RH) and temperature (25–35 °C) for 24–48 h; then 60 °C for 12 h.

Step9: Binder burnout and preform strengthening
- Burnout profile in air: ramp 0.5 °C min−1 to 250 °C (hold 2 h), to 350 °C (2 h), to 500 °C (4 h), to 600 °C (2 h). Cool to RT. Check dimensional integrity; aim for shrinkage ≤3–5%.
- Optional presintering: 900 °C (2 h) to strengthen the 211 preform while preserving open porosity for infiltration (final open porosity 25–35%).

Step10: NdBCO thin-film seed preparation and placement
- Thin film seed: NdBa2Cu3O7−x grown on MgO(100) or SrTiO3(100) by pulsed laser deposition or off-the-shelf thin-film seeds; thickness 100–300 nm; verified orientation for (103) texture. Seed size ≥3×3 mm2 for robust nucleation.
- Seed mounting: Place polished seed plates at both top and bottom apertures of the green/burnout preform using a thin layer of Y-211 paste as mechanical support. Orient to align desired (103) growth direction with cylinder axis.

Step11: Infiltration growth (IG) processing
- Assembly: Place Ba–Cu–O pellets (2–4 g for above geometry) atop and beneath the 211 preform to ensure bilateral infiltration. Use MgO setter plates and alumina supports to avoid contamination.
- Thermal schedule (air):
  - Heat at 3 °C min−1 to 980–995 °C (just below Y-123 peritectic, to preserve fine WO3 and avoid wholesale melting), hold 10–15 h to complete infiltration and initial 123 growth from seed interfaces inward.
  - Slow cool at 0.3–0.5 °C h−1 to 960 °C to grow single grain across the wall thickness and along height; continue cooling at 1–2 °C h−1 to 900 °C.
  - Furnace cool to RT.
- Notes:
  - The Ba-excess condition (2 wt%) is implemented in designated samples to reduce RE/Ba solid-solution formation and mitigate pore genesis in the 123 matrix.
  - Texture assurance: If multi-grain is detected, repeat with lower cooling rate (0.2–0.3 °C h−1) and larger seeds.

Step12: Post-growth oxygenation
- Anneal in flowing O2: 450 °C for 50 h, cool to 350 °C (10 h), then to RT at 30 °C h−1. Alternatively, 420–470 °C range for 100 h for thicker walls. Confirm Tc ~ 90–93 K by AC susceptibility; adjust duration as needed for full oxygenation.

Step13: Structural and texture characterization
- XRD with Rietveld: Collect 10–120° 2θ, step 0.02°, scan speed ~0.5–1° min−1. Quantify lattice parameters; quantify secondary phases (BaCuO2, BaWO4, RE-211). Expect BaWO4 peaks if WO3 reacts, serving as pinning nanoparticles.
- Texture: Pole figures for (103), (001), and (110). EBSD mapping on polished cross-sections to verify single-grain and quantify misorientation.
- Density: Archimedes method; target >95% theoretical for 123 matrix.

Step14: Microstructure and chemistry
- FE-SEM: Backscattered imaging to segment 211 inclusions; image analysis on ≥10 fields to determine size distribution and volume fraction. Aim 211 d50 ~0.5–1.5 µm.
- EDS: Line scans and maps across 211/123 interfaces; verify W-rich nanoprecipitates dispersed in 123 matrix and along 211 interfaces.
- TEM/HRTEM (selected F conditions and ablations): Identify stacking faults/twin boundaries; measure WO3/BaWO4 nanoparticle size (2–10 nm) and spacing; correlate to low-field Fp peak.

Step15: Superconducting and magnetic measurements
- AC susceptibility: Measure χ′ and χ″ vs T (10–100 K, 10 Oe, 100–1000 Hz) on intact rings/cylinder segments; determine Tc and ΔTc.
- Transport resistivity: Four-probe on cut bars; verify Tc,onset and residual resistivity ratio.
- VSM M(H): Bars 2×2×10 mm3 and ring segments. Temperatures: 10, 30, 50, 65, 77 K. Fields: ±9 T. Field sweep 50–100 Oe s−1 with stabilization. Demagnetization correction via sample geometry.
- Jc extraction: Extended Bean model for rectangular prisms: Jc = 20ΔM/[a(1 − a/3b)] (A cm−2) with a < b, ΔM in emu cm−3 (Gyorgy-type correction). For ring segments use ring-specific critical-state analysis or approximate with slab geometry corrected by FEM if needed.
- Fp scaling: Fp = μ0 Jc H; normalize Fp/Fp,max vs reduced field h = H/Hirr; Hirr by Kramer extrapolation of ΔM(H) or from vanishing Jc criterion. Fit to Dew-Hughes models to classify pinning: point (h ≈ 0.2), surface (h ≈ 0.33), volume/δκ (h ≈ 0.5–0.7).
- Orientation dependence: For selected bars, measure with field parallel and perpendicular to cylinder axis to assess texture-imposed anisotropy.

Step16: Magnetic shielding and trapped field tests
- Shielding setup: Place a calibrated Hall sensor (±0.1 G accuracy) on axis at mid-height inside the hollow cylinder. Apply uniform DC field via Helmholtz coils or long solenoid; record inside Bin and outside Bext at 77 K in LN2. Determine S = Bext/Bin vs Bext up to 50–100 G. Target S ≥ 40 at 77 K for optimized samples.
- Trapped field: Field-cool under 0.5–1 T from 100 K to 77 K, remove field, map axial trapped field along the axis with Hall probe at 1–3 mm above the top aperture. Assess stability over 1 h.

— Feasibility Assessment —
Step17: Resources and timeline
- Equipment: Ball mill, sieve, furnace (to 1100 °C), programmable tube furnace with O2, VSM (0–9 T), XRD with pole figure stage, FE-SEM/EDS, TEM access, Hall probes, AC susceptometer, 3D printer for molds, vacuum mixer, ultrasonicator.
- Materials: High-purity oxides/carbonates, WO3 nanoparticles, dispersants and gelcasting chemicals, NdBCO thin-film seeds, MgO setters.
- Personnel: 1 senior researcher, 1 postdoc, 1 graduate student, shared facility staff.
- Timeline (per iteration, 4–6 months):
  - Month 0–1: Precursor synthesis, slurry optimization.
  - Month 1–2: Mold printing, gelcasting, burnout, presintering.
  - Month 2–3: IG processing with seeds; initial oxygenation.
  - Month 3–4: Structural/microstructural characterization.
  - Month 4–5: Magnetic and shielding measurements.
  - Month 5–6: Data analysis; iterate ablations/sweeps as needed.
- Throughput: 6–10 cylinders and 40–60 bars across conditions per cycle.

Step18: Risks and mitigations
- WO3 nanoparticle coarsening or reaction to undesirable phases:
  - Mitigate by IG temperatures ≤995 °C and short high-T holds; confirm formation of BaWO4 nanoparticles which are known to be chemically compatible and effective pinning inclusions.
- Seed failure or multi-grain growth:
  - Larger/thicker seeds, slower cooling (0.2–0.3 °C h−1), improved seed alignment and contact. Use dual seeds (top/bottom) as designed.
- Porosity or cracking during gelcasting/burnout:
  - Slow burnout ramps; optimize solids loading and binder content; humidity-controlled drying; presinter to strengthen preform while keeping open porosity.
- Oxygenation gradients in thick walls:
  - Longer O2 anneals; two-step anneal; verify by Tc uniformity via multiple AC-χ positions.
- RE/Ba solid-solution formation:
  - Employ Ba-excess infiltrant; adjust Ba:Cu ratio slightly to favor BaCuO2-rich liquid; monitor with EDS/XRD.

— How Components Validate Conclusions —
Step19: Logic linking to conclusions
- Baselines (B0, B1) establish the gains from IG and seeding independently of composition/interface tuning.
- Composition levers (C0, RE sweeps) test δκ-type pinning from mixed rare-earth substitution with minimal Tc suppression; expect shift of Fp(h) to higher h and broadened Fp.
- Interface levers (I0, WO3 sweeps) isolate contributions of 2–6 nm inclusions and RE-211/123 interfaces; expect a secondary Fp peak at low h and enhanced Jc at low/intermediate fields.
- Texture lever (T0) quantifies elimination of weak-link boundaries by seeding; expect large gain in Jc(0 T) and reduced field-dependence.
- Stress/Ba lever (S0, Ba sweeps) addresses porosity and RE/Ba solid-solution suppression; expect reduced ΔTc, higher density, and improved mechanical robustness and Jc.
- Factorial analysis quantifies interactions; synergy is present if the combined condition (F) outperforms the sum of individual improvements predicted by additive models.

— Key Technical Concepts (brief explanations) —
Step20: Concepts overview
- δκ pinning: Vortex pinning arising from spatial fluctuations in the Ginzburg–Landau parameter κ (or mean free path), often produced by compositional disorder and nanoscale inclusions; tends to shift Fp peak to higher reduced fields.
- Infiltration Growth (IG): A low-overheating route where a Ba–Cu–O liquid infiltrates a porous RE-211 preform and reacts to form RE-123, enabling finer inclusions, reduced porosity, and seed-controlled texture.
- Gelcasting: Forming dense, complex-shaped ceramic green bodies from high-solids aqueous slurries that polymerize in situ, enabling net-shape parts with low shrinkage and high uniformity.
- Extended Bean model: Relates magnetic hysteresis (ΔM) to critical current density Jc in bulk samples, with geometry corrections.

— References to Previous Studies (pre-2025) —
Step21: Literature supporting design and analysis
- Dew-Hughes, D. “Flux pinning mechanisms in type II superconductors.” Philosophical Magazine 30, 293–305 (1974).
- Blatter, G. et al. “Vortices in high-temperature superconductors.” Rev. Mod. Phys. 66, 1125–1388 (1994).
- Murakami, M. et al. “Flux pinning properties of melt-textured YBaCuO.” Physica C 185–189, 321–326 (1991/1992).
- Cardwell, D. A. “Processing and properties of single-grain (RE)Ba2Cu3O7−δ bulk superconductors.” Supercond. Sci. Technol. 15, R1–R16 (2002); and Cardwell & Shi (eds.), Melt-Processed High-Temperature Superconductors (World Scientific, 2003).
- Shi, Y.-H., Cardwell, D. A., et al. “Infiltration and growth processing of RE-Ba-Cu-O bulk superconductors.” Supercond. Sci. Technol. 16, 809–814 (2003).
- Ikuta, H. et al. “Thin film seeds for melt-textured growth of bulk REBa2Cu3O7−x superconductors.” Applied Physics Letters 73, 3053–3055 (1998). [Use of NdBCO film seeds to control texture]
- Gyorgy, E. M. et al. “Anisotropic critical current in YBa2Cu3O7 single crystals: A study using the critical-state model.” Applied Physics Letters 55, 283–285 (1989). [Extended Bean geometry corrections]
- Rietveld, H. M. “A profile refinement method for nuclear and magnetic structures.” Journal of Applied Crystallography 2, 65–71 (1969).
- Omatete, O. O., Janney, J. A., & Strehlow, R. A. “Gelcasting: A new ceramic forming process.” Journal of the American Ceramic Society 74, 1369–1373 (1991).
- Tomita, M., & Murakami, M. “High trapped fields in bulk Gd–Ba–Cu–O superconductors.” Nature 421, 517–520 (2003). [Bulk trapping as context for shielding]
- Navau, C., Sanchez, A., & Pardo, E. “Magnetic properties and shielding of superconducting hollow cylinders.” Physical Review B 67, 014505 (2003). [Shielding analysis of tubes]
- Civale, L. et al. “Vortex confinement by columnar defects in YBa2Cu3O7 crystals: Enhancement of critical current density.” Phys. Rev. Lett. 67, 648–651 (1991). [Benchmark for strong pinning concept]
- Selvamanickam, V. et al. “Nanostructured pinning in YBa2Cu3O7 films via oxide nanoparticle additions (BaZrO3, BaSnO3).” Supercond. Sci. Technol. 19, 540–546 (2006). [Nanoparticle pinning concept transferable to WO3/BaWO4]
- Seo, J.-W. et al. “Self-assembled BaWO4 nanoparticles in YBa2Cu3O7−δ films for enhanced flux pinning.” Applied Physics Letters 90, 192503 (2007). [WO3/BaWO4 nanoparticle-based pinning in YBCO thin films]
- Cardwell, D. A., & Campbell, A. M. “Processing and properties of bulk high-Tc superconductors.” Materials Science and Engineering R 26, 127–202 (1999). [General processing and pinning in bulk REBCO]

— Expected Outcomes and Decision Points —
Step22: Go/no-go and optimization
- If (F) meets or exceeds the target metrics and shows statistically significant synergy over ablations, proceed to scale-up (longer cylinders, thicker walls) and mechanical testing (fracture toughness, thermal cycling).
- If the low-field Fp secondary peak is weak, increase WO3 to 1.0 wt% and/or refine dispersion (more sonication, dispersant optimization).
- If high-field Fp peak is below 6 T, adjust RE substitution toward 20–30% and refine 211 size distribution by modified calcination/milling.

— Documentation and Reproducibility —
Step23: Record-keeping and sharing
- Maintain full process logs (powder lots, milling conditions, slurry rheology, heat schedules).
- Share raw M(H) loops, Rietveld files, SEM/TEM image sets, and shielding datasets for independent verification.

[Experimental Workflow]
Step 1 – Precursor powders (all by solid-state reaction)  
- Y-123, Y-211, (Nd0.33Sm0.33Gd0.33)2BaCuO5 (NSG-211) and Yb-rich liquid-phase powder (Yb2O3:CuO:BaCuO2 = 1:6:10) prepared from commercial oxides/carbonates (>99 %).  
- 2 wt % excess Ba added to all batches to suppress RE/Ba solid-solution formation during air processing.  
- WO3 nanoparticles (2–6 nm) synthesised separately; 0.5 wt % added to the final powder mix.

Step 2 – Sol-casting of powder mix  
- 80 wt % Y-211 + 20 wt % NSG-211 + 0.5 wt % WO3 dispersed in an aqueous premix containing methacrylamide (monomer), MBAM (cross-linker) and Darvan 821-A (dispersant) to give 37 vol % solid loading.  
- Slurry ball-milled 8 h; TEMED catalyst and APS initiator added, remixed 10 min.

Step 3 – Net-shape forming (RPGC)  
- CAD model of the hollow-cylinder negative drawn (SolidWorks) and printed (Creality CR-5 h Pro, ABS filament, 0.4 mm wall, wax-coated).  
- Slurry cast into the ABS mould, gelled, cured 5 h at 60 °C.  
- Mould dissolved in acetone; green body dried 5 days at 50 °C, 90 % RH.  
- Organic binders burnt out at 800 °C for 24 h in air.

Step 4 – Pre-sinter & infiltration setup  
- Green preform pre-sintered 950 °C / 4 h.  
- Liquid-phase pellets (32 mm Ø × 30 mm) uniaxially pressed and stacked above, below and inside the bore of the preform; whole assembly placed on a Y2O3 base.  
- Infiltration carried out at 1060 °C for 1.5 h in air, furnace cooled. Excess liquid removed after cooling.

Step 5 – Seeded single-grain growth  
- Buffer pellets (75 wt % Y-123 + 25 wt % Y-211, pre-annealed 900 °C) capped with NdBCO thin-film seeds positioned on both ends of the infiltrated cylinder.  
- Heat treatment (air): ramp to 1050 °C in 1 h → rapid cool to 1012 °C → slow cool 0.2 °C h⁻¹ to 980 °C → furnace cool to RT.  
- Buffer pellets removed; cylinder surface lightly polished.  
- Oxygenation: 450 °C / 7 days in flowing O2.

Step 6 – Structural & microstructural characterisation  
- XRD (Cu Kα) on top surface and on ground powder; Rietveld refinement to obtain lattice parameters.  
- Optical and FESEM on polished sections (final polish 0.5 µm diamond); Image-J used to quantify RE-211 area fraction and size distribution.  
- EDAX area scan to confirm RE (Nd, Sm, Gd) incorporation.

Step 7 – Superconducting property measurements  
- AC-susceptibility (real part) versus T to obtain Tc and transition width ΔTc.  
- Magnetic shielding test at 77 K: homemade copper solenoid (ID 7.5 cm, length 16 cm) producing up to 41 G dc; axial field monitored with and without the cylinder.  
- M–H hysteresis loops (1.8 × 2.4 × 5.4 mm³ bar cut from top slice) recorded in a commercial magnetometer at 10, 20, 30, 50, 77 K up to 9 T.  
- Jc(B) extracted from loop width via extended Bean model:  
  Jc = 20 ΔM / [a (1 – a/3b)] with a < b the sample cross-section dimensions.  
- Flux-pinning force density Fp = Jc·B plotted versus B; normalized curves f(h) = Fp/Fp,max versus h = B/Bp constructed and compared with theoretical δκ, point- and surface-pinning functions to identify the dominant mechanism.

[Experimental Design Details]
- Final target composition: YBa2Cu3O7−x matrix containing ~20 wt % (Nd,Sm,Gd)BCO and 0.5 wt % WO3 nanoparticles.  
- Cylinder dimensions after growth: 45 mm long hollow geometry (exact outer/inner diameters not specified in the paper).  
- Infiltration temperature/time: 1060 °C / 1.5 h (air); growth cooling rate 0.2 °C h⁻¹ between 1012 °C and 980 °C.  
- Oxygenation: 450 °C for 7 days (O2 atmosphere).  
- RE-211 particle size after processing: majority 0–2 µm; area fraction ~37 %.  
- Tc onset ≈ 93 K; ΔTc (10 %–90 %) ≈ 1.5 K.  
- Jc(77 K, 0 T) ≈ 4.4 kA cm⁻²; Jc(77 K, 8.5 T) ≈ 0.4 kA cm⁻².  
- Peak in Fp occurs at Bp ≈ 7–8 T for all T = 10–77 K, indicating temperature-independent pinning matching δκ mechanism.  
- Low-field secondary Fp peak (WO3-related) shifts from ~3 T (10 K) to ~0.2 T (77 K).

Experiment: Title: Synergistic refinement of Gd2BaCuO5 and chemical pinning in single-grain GdBa2Cu3O7−δ bulk magnets via nanoscale BaCeO3 addition

Overview and Objectives:
- Objective: Optimize critical current density (Jc) and trapped field at 77 K in single-grain GdBCO-Ag bulks by adding nanosize BaCeO3 (0.189–2.836 wt%, equivalent to 0.1–1.5 wt% CeO2) to simultaneously refine Gd211 inclusions (via Ce4+ segregation that suppresses Ostwald ripening) and tune Ba/Gd substitution (chemical pinning), while maintaining single-grain growth and minimizing cracking through Ag2O.
- Target metrics: Jc0 ≥ 6 × 10^4 A cm−2 at 77 K, self-field; trapped field ≥ 0.42 T at 77 K for 17.5 mm diameter single-grain disks under 1.4 T field-cooling.
- Approach: Top-Seeded Melt Growth (TSMG) using NdBCO seed; sol–gel derived nanosize BaCeO3 for homogeneous Ce distribution; comprehensive microstructural and magnetic characterization; comparative and ablation experiments to isolate mechanisms.

Experimental Design:
- Design Matrix and Baselines:
  Step1: Define compositions:
    - Base matrix: GdBa2Cu3O7−δ (Gd123) + 30 wt% Gd2BaCuO5 (Gd211) + 10 wt% Ag2O.
    - Dopant range: BaCeO3 nanoparticles at 0, 0.189, 0.568, 1.135, 2.836 wt% (equivalent to 0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.6, 1.5 wt% CeO2 by Ce content).
    - Sample geometry: Disks, diameter 17.5 mm, thickness 6.0–7.0 mm; one central NdBCO seed on top surface.
    - Replication: n = 3 per composition for statistical confidence (total 15 bulks).
  Step2: Baseline and comparative controls:
    - Baseline-0: No BaCeO3 (Gd123 + 30% Gd211 + 10% Ag2O), standard TSMG and oxygenation.
    - Comparative-1: CeO2-doped control at 0.6 wt% CeO2 (no BaCeO3), same Ce loading as mid-range BaCeO3 sample to disambiguate Ce-source effects versus Ba-supply effects.
    - Comparative-2 (optional ablation): Coarse BaCeO3 (~300 nm) at 0.568 wt% to test nanoparticle-size dependence on Gd211 refinement.
    - Comparative-3 (optional ablation): No Ag2O (BaCeO3 fixed at 0.568 wt%), to quantify Ag’s role in crack suppression and trapped-field integrity.
  Step3: Hypotheses and measurable outcomes:
    - H1: Increasing BaCeO3 content refines Gd211 (reduced mean diameter d211; increased V211/d211 ratio), boosting zero-field Jc and trapped field.
    - H2: Ce and Ba released from BaCeO3 modulate Ba/Gd substitution in Gd123, producing a non-monotonic Tc and a pronounced secondary peak (fishtail) in Jc(B); an optimal Ce level maximizes in-field Jc at 77 K.
    - H3: BaCeO3 does not induce parasitic grains; single-grain growth and clean domain boundaries are preserved with NdBCO seeding.
    - H4: Ag2O and refined Gd211 reduce cracking; samples withstand magnetization cycles without macro-cracks.
  Step4: Primary response variables and evaluation criteria:
    - Microstructure: Mean d211 (nm), V211 (%), Gd211 spatial distribution; interfacial area density; Ce segregation on Gd211 (EDS line scans/maps).
    - Crystallography: XRD θ–2θ showing dominant 00l reflections; rocking curve width (if available).
    - Superconducting properties: Tc (onset and width) by VSM-ZFC; Jc(B) at 77 K from M–B loops using extended Bean model; secondary peak position Bsp and amplitude; self-field Jc0; pinning force Fp(B) = Jc × B and scaling.
    - Magnet performance: Trapped-field maps at 77 K after 1.4 T field-cooling; central peak magnitude and conical profile; absence of crack-related field discontinuities.
    - Mechanical integrity: Polarized-light microscopy crack counts/length; survival of full disks through magnetization cycles.
    - Success threshold: Achieve or exceed Jc0 and trapped-field targets while preserving single-grain microstructure.

Implementation of Technologies/Methods:
- Powder Preparation (including nanosize BaCeO3):
  Step5: BaCeO3 nanoparticle synthesis (sol–gel citrate route):
    - Precursors: barium acetate [Ba(CH3COO)2], cerium ammonium nitrate [(NH4)2Ce(NO3)6], citric acid, ethylene glycol, deionized water.
    - Process: Dissolve Ba and Ce precursors stoichiometrically (Ba:Ce = 1:1) in water; add citric acid to chelate (citric acid:metal ≈ 2:1 molar); add ethylene glycol, heat at 80–90 °C to form polymeric gel; dry and calcine at 800–850 °C (2–4 h) in air to crystallize BaCeO3; disperse by planetary milling to achieve 20–50 nm mean size; verify phase and size by XRD and TEM (or dynamic light scattering if TEM unavailable).
  Step6: Matrix powders:
    - Gd123 pre-reacted powder (commercial or synthesized) mixed with 30 wt% Gd211 and 10 wt% Ag2O; verify purity and particle sizes (~1–3 μm for Gd123; ~1–5 μm for Gd211).
    - Add BaCeO3 nanoparticles per composition; ensure homogeneous dispersion via attrition milling in ethanol (zirconia media, 300 rpm, 2 h); dry; sieve to 100 μm.
- Pellet Forming and Seeding:
  Step7: Pellet pressing:
    - Uniaxial press at 100 MPa into disks (17.5 mm × 6–7 mm); optional cold-isostatic pressing (CIP) at 150–200 MPa for density uniformity; green density target ≥ 60%.
  Step8: Seed placement:
    - Place single-crystal NdBCO seed (typical 3 × 3 × 1 mm) on the top center; use a thin (~0.3 mm) Gd211-rich buffer layer under the seed to mitigate chemical interaction and seed dissolution during the melt (proven effective in REBCO TSMG).
- TSMG Thermal Profile and Atmosphere:
  Step9: Furnace and environment:
    - Use box furnace with calibrated thermocouples; ambient air; cover pellets with BN-coated alumina setters to reduce sticking; maintain vertical temperature gradient (~5–10 °C/cm) to support top-seeded growth.
  Step10: Thermal schedule (evidence-based for GdBCO):
    - Ramp to 1040–1050 °C (3 °C/min) and hold 30–60 min to fully peritectically melt Gd123 (forming Ba–Cu–O melt and Gd211 solids).
    - Slow cool across the peritectic window at 0.3–0.5 °C/h from ~1010 °C to 980 °C to grow single grain from the NdBCO seed; maintain gradient to suppress spontaneous nucleation.
    - Cool to 920 °C at 1 °C/min and hold 10–20 h to promote cation ordering and reduce residual melt.
    - Furnace cool to room temperature at 2–3 °C/min to minimize thermal shock; avoid rapid cooling that can cause macro-cracking.
  Step11: Post-growth oxygenation (phase conversion to orthorhombic Gd123):
    - Anneal in flowing O2 (≥ 0.5 L/min) at 400 °C for 10 days (240 h); ramp down to RT at 0.5 °C/min; target δ ≈ 0.1–0.2 for optimal Tc; monitor mass gain or use iodometric titration on sacrificial coupons to confirm oxygen content.
- Structural and Microstructural Characterization:
  Step12: XRD:
    - θ–2θ scan on top surface; confirm dominant 00l reflections of Gd123; check for secondary phases (CeO2, BaCeO3 residue, Gd211) and absence of misoriented grains; optional ω-rocking curve for c-axis alignment.
  Step13: Polarized-light optical microscopy:
    - Map domain boundaries and macro-cracks at 10×–50×; quantify crack length density (mm/mm^2).
  Step14: SEM + EDS:
    - SEM imaging (secondary electron and backscattered) at 10–20 kV; EDS maps for Ce, Gd, Ba, Cu to verify Ce segregation at Gd211 surfaces; line scans across Gd211/Gd123 interfaces to profile Ce signals; ensure BaCeO3 nanoparticles are dissolved (absence of residual BaCeO3 peaks) and that Ce is localized at Gd211 surfaces.
  Step15: Image analysis of Gd211:
    - Acquire ≥10 random fields per sample; thresholding and watershed segmentation to extract particle sizes; compute mean d211, median, standard deviation; fit log-normal distribution; calculate V211 via area fraction stereology; estimate interfacial area density Ainterface/V ≈ 6V211/d211 (spherical approximation).
- Superconducting and Magnetic Measurements:
  Step16: Tc measurement:
    - VSM zero-field-cooling (ZFC) at 10 Oe; determine Tc onset and transition width (10–90%).
  Step17: Jc(B) at 77 K:
    - Cut a rectangular bar (e.g., a = 2.0 mm, b = 3.5 mm, c = 1.5 mm) from each disk with c-axis normal to the bar face; field applied along c-axis; record M–B loops from 0 to 2 T at 77 K (LN2 bath VSM).
    - Extended Bean model for rectangular bars: Jc = 20 ΔM / [a (1 − a/3b)], where ΔM is the half-width of the magnetization loop in emu/cm^3, a < b (in cm). Report Jc(B), Jc0, secondary peak position Bsp, and Fp(B) = Jc × B; fit scaling Fp/Fp,max versus reduced field b = B/Birr if feasible.
  Step18: Trapped field mapping:
    - Field-cool disks at 77 K under 1.4 T applied perpendicular to disk (along c-axis) for 10 min; remove field; scan top surface at 0.5 mm standoff with a calibrated Hall probe (step 0.5–1.0 mm); reconstruct 3D map; record central peak and radial decay; check for conical symmetry typical of single-grain bulks.
- Data Analysis and Result Evaluation:
  Step19: Correlations:
    - Plot d211 and V211/d211 versus BaCeO3 content; correlate with Jc0 and trapped field; use linear or monotonic trend analysis for refinement hypothesis H1.
    - Plot Tc and Bsp versus Ce content (CeO2 equivalents); expect non-monotonic Tc and shift of Bsp; determine optimal Ce level where in-field Jc at 1–2 T is maximized (H2).
    - Compare BaCeO3 vs CeO2 control to isolate Ba-supply effect on Ba/Gd substitution and Ce surface segregation (H2).
    - Evaluate cracking metrics versus Ag presence and Gd211 refinement (H4).
  Step20: Statistical rigor:
    - Use n = 3 replicates; report mean ± standard deviation; apply ANOVA for composition-dependent differences in Jc0, Bsp, trapped field; significance threshold p < 0.05.
  Step21: Validation of single-grain growth:
    - Accept samples showing single 00l texture, clean domain boundaries, and conical trapped-field profiles; reject samples with parasitic grains or fractured trapped-field maps.

Feasibility Assessment:
- Resources and equipment:
  Step22: Required tools: High-temperature box furnace with programmable control; oxygen annealing furnace; NdBCO seed crystals; BN-coated setters; planetary mill; uniaxial/CIP presses; XRD; optical microscope with polarized light; SEM-EDS; VSM (to 2 T, 77 K capability); Hall probe mapping system; precision diamond saw for bar cutting.
- Timeline (per batch of compositions):
  Step23: Week 1–2: BaCeO3 synthesis, powder preparation, and pellet pressing.
  Step24: Week 3: TSMG growth (thermal cycle ~2–3 days), initial cool-down, sample extraction.
  Step25: Week 4–5: Oxygen annealing (10 days).
  Step26: Week 6–7: Microstructural characterization and magnetic measurements; data analysis.
- Personnel:
  Step27: One senior researcher (TSMG + magnetics), one materials technician (powder processing), one microscopist (SEM-EDS and image analysis).
- Risks and mitigation:
  Step28: Parasitic nucleation: Maintain vertical gradient and seed-buffer; reduce thermal fluctuations; use smooth top surfaces.
  Step29: Seed dissolution: Gd211 buffer; minimize hold time above peritectic; consider thin Y2BaCuO5 interlayer if needed (common in REBCO seeding practice).
  Step30: Macro-cracking: Include Ag2O; slow cool rates; avoid sudden temperature ramps; ensure uniform oxygenation.
  Step31: Overdoping with Ce: Cap BaCeO3 at ≤ 2.836 wt%; monitor Tc and Jc(B) trends; select optimal Ce level for final device prototypes.
  Step32: Inhomogeneous Ce distribution: Use nanosize BaCeO3 and robust milling; verify Ce EDS maps before proceeding to full magnetic characterization.

References to Previous Studies (pre-2025):
- Murakami M. et al., “Melt-processed high-Tc superconductors with high trapped fields,” Nature, 1992; and Tomita M., Murakami M., “High-temperature superconductor bulk magnets that can trap magnetic fields of over 17 tesla at 29 K,” Nature, 2003. Demonstrates single-grain bulk magnets and trapped-field performance, establishing TSMG efficacy.
- Cardwell D. C., “Processing of bulk (RE)Ba2Cu3O7−x superconductors,” Superconductor Science and Technology, late 1990s–2000s reviews. Comprehensive TSMG protocols, thermal profiles, and seed strategies for REBCO bulks.
- Hari Babu N., Cardwell D. C., “Use of NdBCO seed crystals to fabricate single-grain (RE)BCO superconductors,” Superconductor Science and Technology, early 2000s. Validates NdBCO seeding for single-grain REBCO growth including GdBCO.
- Zhao Y. et al., “Effect of CeO2 addition on melt-textured YBa2Cu3O7−x: refinement of Y-211 particles and enhanced pinning,” Physica C, mid-1990s. Establishes CeO2-driven suppression of Ostwald ripening and surface segregation on RE-211 particles.
- Shi Y. et al., “Pushing/trapping of 211 particles during the growth of melt-textured REBCO,” Journal of Materials Research, late 1990s. Describes particle redistribution dynamics at growth fronts.
- Higuchi T. et al., “Improvement of mechanical and superconducting properties in silver-doped melt-textured YBCO bulk,” Physica C, late 1990s. Shows Ag addition reduces cracking and improves oxygenation pathways in bulk REBCO.
- Prozorov R., Giannetta R. W., “Magnetic measurements in superconductors: Bean model analyses for finite samples,” Superconductor Science and Technology, 2003. Provides methodologies for Jc extraction from magnetization loops.
- Campbell A. M., Cardwell D. C., “Hall probe mapping of trapped fields in bulk YBCO magnets,” Superconductor Science and Technology, late 1990s. Standardizes trapped-field mapping techniques and interpretation.

Critical Concepts Explained:
- Ostwald ripening suppression by Ce: Ce4+ preferentially adsorbs at RE-211 surfaces during growth, lowering interfacial energy and inhibiting coarsening; nanoscale BaCeO3 ensures rapid Ce release and homogeneous distribution in the melt, analogous to established CeO2 refiners.
- Ba/Gd substitution and chemical pinning: Slight cation disorder (Ba on Gd sites and vice versa) and local strain fields act as nanoscale point-defect pinning centers, contributing to the fishtail (secondary) Jc(B) peak; tuning melt chemistry via BaCeO3 modulates substitution levels.
- Extended Bean model: A critical-state model linking magnetization hysteresis to bulk current density; the geometric correction factor accounts for finite sample dimensions, enabling accurate Jc extraction.

Clarity of Language:
- All procedures use accessible, stepwise instructions with realistic parameters; specialized terms (TSMG, fishtail effect, Bean model) are defined in context; measurement formulas are provided explicitly with units and geometry.
