Title: Face-to-face double-stacked (FFDS) REBCO coated conductors with complementary angular Ic profiles: fabrication, current-sharing interface control, and anisotropy minimization

Objectives
- Fabricate REBCO coated conductors on IBAD-MgO/LaMnO3 (LMO) buffered Hastelloy C‑276 with high in-plane texture (Δφ ≈ 6–7°).
- Deposit YBa2Cu3O7−δ (YBCO) and EuBa2Cu3O7−δ (EuBCO) layers; introduce 3.5 mol% BaHfO3 (BHO) nanorod artificial pinning centers (APCs) into the EuBCO layer to enhance Jc at B parallel to c-axis (B//c).
- Assemble face-to-face soldered double stacks (FFDS) using a 2–4 μm Sn63Pb37 interlayer to achieve interfacial contact resistivity near 2 nΩ·cm².
- Quantitatively demonstrate that Ic,FFDS(θ) ≈ Ic,YBCO(θ) + Ic,EuBCO+BHO(θ) at 65 K, 1.5 T, and that angular anisotropy is reduced (lower standard deviation and higher minimum Ic).
- Extract interface resistance per unit length by fitting an equivalent-circuit model to transport I–V data, and map its influence on current sharing and anisotropy.

Section A. Experimental Design

A1. Sample matrix and comparisons
- Single tapes (baselines):
  - YBCO/LMO/IBAD-MgO/Hastelloy (single-layer).
  - EuBCO+3.5 mol% BHO/LMO/IBAD-MgO/Hastelloy (single-layer).
- FFDS stacks (target and controls):
  - FFDS-solder: YBCO facing EuBCO+BHO, bonded with 2–4 μm Sn63Pb37 (low Rc target).
  - FFDS-insulated control: same pair face-to-face with 5–10 μm epoxy spacer (no electrical contact) to isolate purely magnetic/mechanical coupling (no current sharing).
  - FFDS-thick solder control: 10–15 μm Sn63Pb37 to test the effect of increased interface resistivity and current transfer length.
  - FFDS-mismatched: YBCO//YBCO and EuBCO+BHO//EuBCO+BHO stacks (to verify complementarity is the driver of anisotropy reduction).
- Texture ablation:
  - Repeat YBCO and EuBCO+BHO on IBAD templates with slightly degraded in-plane texture (Δφ ≈ 9–10°) to probe texture dependence.
- APC ablation:
  - EuBCO without BHO (0 mol%) to isolate the role of BHO nanorods.
- Interface-resistance ablations:
  - FFDS with slightly oxidized surfaces prior to soldering (Rc↑).
  - FFDS with Ni/Au flash metallization prior to soldering (Rc↓).

A2. Measurement conditions and metrics
- Temperature and field: 65 K, 1.5 T, DC field; additional points at 77 K, 1–3 T for mapping.
- Angle: θ from −40° to 220° with 2° steps; θ = 0° is B//c; θ = 90° is B//ab.
- Transport methodology: 4-probe I–V, 1 μV/cm electric field criterion for Ic; n-value from E = Ec (I/Ic)^n fits between 0.1 and 10 μV/cm; minimum current transfer length (≥10 cm gauge length) for FFDS.
- Primary metrics:
  - Ic(θ), Ic,min, Ic,max; angular standard deviation σ(Ic)/⟨Ic⟩; anisotropy ratio Ic,max/Ic,min.
  - For stacks: ΔIc(θ) ≡ Ic,FFDS(θ) − [Ic,YBCO(θ) + Ic,EuBCO+BHO(θ)].
  - Extracted interface contact resistivity ρc (Ω·cm²) and per-unit-length Rc (Ω·m⁻¹).
  - n-values for each orientation.
- Statistical reliability: n = 3–5 samples per condition; report mean ± standard deviation; use ANOVA/t-tests for significance (p < 0.05).

A3. Step-by-step workflow
1. Substrate/template procurement and qualification:
   - IBAD-MgO buffered Hastelloy C-276 tapes with LMO cap; verify Δφ = 6–7° by LMO (200) φ-scan.
2. PLD deposition (YBCO; EuBCO; EuBCO+BHO):
   - Calibrate growth for dense epitaxial films; thickness 0.8–1.0 μm REBCO; LMO cap 20–30 nm.
3. Microstructure and texture characterization:
   - XRD (θ–2θ, ω-rocking, φ-scans), TEM/STEM for BHO nanorods (density, diameter, alignment).
4. Single-tape transport:
   - Ic(θ) at 65 K, 1.5 T; obtain baseline curves for YBCO and EuBCO(+/−BHO).
5. FFDS assembly:
   - Reel-to-reel soldering at 200 °C with Sn63Pb37 (2–4 μm).
   - Prepare controls (insulated, thick solder, metallized).
6. FFDS transport and modeling:
   - Ic(θ) for each FFDS; compare to arithmetic sum of single tapes.
   - Full I–V curves at key angles (θ = 0°, 45°, 90°) for model fitting and Rc extraction.
7. Additional diagnostics:
   - Magneto-optical imaging (MOI) at 77 K for qualitative current redistribution at near‑Ic regimes.
   - Contact resistivity of lap-joint coupons to cross-check ρc.
8. Data analysis and validation:
   - Evaluate anisotropy metrics; test hypothesis that FFDS reduces σ(Ic)/⟨Ic⟩ and lifts Ic,min.
   - Sensitivity analysis versus Rc, Δφ, and BHO content using ablation sets.

A4. Validation logic
- Baselines define intrinsic angular profiles of each tape.
- The insulated FFDS control confirms that simple parallel magnetic coupling or mechanical contact does not change Ic; any Ic improvement in soldered FFDS is due to electrical current sharing.
- Thick-solder and oxidized-surface ablations increase Rc and should degrade current-sharing effectiveness; anisotropy reduction should track Rc.
- APC ablations verify that c-axis enhancement arises from BHO nanorods.
- Texture ablations confirm that maintaining Δφ ≈ 6–7° preserves ab-plane performance while enabling complementary c-axis gain.
- Model-extracted Rc is cross-validated by direct lap-joint contact-resistivity coupons.

Section B. Implementation of Technologies/Methods

B1. Substrates and buffer/cap stack
- Substrate: Hastelloy C‑276, 50–100 μm thick.
- IBAD-MgO template with seed/buffer stack from qualified vendor; top cap LaMnO3, 20–30 nm.
- Texture: verify Δφ(200) of LMO by XRD four-circle φ-scan; target 6–7° FWHM.

B2. PLD growth of superconducting layers
- Deposition tool: reel-to-reel PLD with KrF (248 nm) excimer laser.
- Base REBCO compositions: YBa2Cu3O7−δ and EuBa2Cu3O7−δ.
- Targets:
  - YBCO: stoichiometric ceramic, >97% density.
  - EuBCO: stoichiometric ceramic.
  - EuBCO+BHO: composite target with 3.5 mol% BaHfO3 second-phase; or dual-target co-ablation calibrated to net 3.5 mol%.
- Growth parameters (evidence-based ranges for epitaxial, nanorod-forming films):
  - Substrate temperature: 770–790 °C.
  - Oxygen partial pressure: 150–250 mTorr during growth.
  - Laser fluence: 1.5–2.0 J/cm² at 5–10 Hz.
  - Film thickness: 0.8–1.0 μm REBCO.
  - Post-deposition oxygenation: 450–500 °C in 500–600 Torr O2 for 30–60 min; slow cool to ensure δ ≈ 0–0.2.
- BHO nanorod formation:
  - The immiscible perovskite BaHfO3 phase nucleates as c-axis aligned nanorods under PLD’s far-from-equilibrium kinetics; 3.5 mol% yields rod diameters ~3–5 nm and spacings ~10–20 nm, optimized for c-axis correlated pinning without excessive Tc suppression as demonstrated for similar BaZrO3/BaHfO3 systems.

B3. Microstructural and texture characterization
- XRD:
  - θ–2θ scans to confirm c-axis oriented REBCO (00l) peaks.
  - ω-rocking curves of (005) or (00l) reflections: target FWHM ≤ 1.0°.
  - φ-scans of REBCO (103) and LMO (200): target Δφ ≈ 6–7° for LMO; ensure cube texture transfer.
- TEM/STEM:
  - Cross-sectional TEM to visualize BHO nanorods (vertical alignment, density).
  - STEM-EDS/EELS to confirm Hf-containing rods and clean REBCO matrix.
- AFM/SEM:
  - Surface morphology to assess particulates and roughness (Rq < 5 nm typical).

B4. FFDS assembly with solder interface
- Surface preparation:
  - Clean REBCO surfaces with low-power Ar ion beam or solvent rinse to remove adventitious contamination; avoid damaging REBCO.
  - Optional 50–100 nm Au flash on REBCO to promote wetting and reduce oxide formation for Rc-reduction ablation set.
- Solder: Sn63Pb37 eutectic, melting at 183 °C.
- Deposition of solder layer:
  - Physical coating: thermal evaporation or ultrasonic solder deposition to 2–4 μm thickness per side; thickness verified by profilometry.
- Lamination:
  - Reel-to-reel hot pressing at 200 °C under 0.3–0.5 MPa, 2–5 min dwell, in dry N2 to limit oxidation; aligned “face-to-face” so both REBCO layers contact through solder.
  - Cool at ≤2 °C/s to minimize thermal stress.
- Controls:
  - Insulated FFDS: 5–10 μm epoxy (e.g., non-conductive polyimide) spacer instead of solder.
  - Thick solder: 10–15 μm SnPb to modify current transfer length and Rc.

B5. Electrical contact resistivity characterization (cross-check)
- Lap-joint coupon method:
  - Overlap length 20–50 mm; width 4–6 mm; four-probe measurement at 77 K and 65 K; derive contact resistivity ρc = Rcontact·A, where A is bonded area.
  - Target ρc ≈ 1–5 nΩ·cm² for optimized stacks.

B6. Transport measurement and angular rig
- Samples: 10–15 cm long, 4–6 mm wide.
- Voltage taps:
  - Soldered copper taps spaced 50–80 mm; low-thermal EMF wires; ensure taps on both tapes for differential measurements in FFDS.
- Cryostat/magnet:
  - Variable-temperature cryostat set to 65.0 ± 0.2 K; superconducting split-pair magnet at 1.5 T; sample rotator with ±0.5° accuracy.
- I–V acquisition:
  - Ramp current up to exceed Ic by 10–20% at each angle; capture E–I to extract n-values.
  - Criterion: Ic at Ec = 1 μV/cm.
- Current partition measurement (optional):
  - Differential taps on each side of FFDS to estimate the fraction of current in each tape from small potential differences, providing direct evidence of redistribution when one tape enters flux flow.

B7. Equivalent-circuit model and Rc extraction
- Model structure:
  - Two nonlinear branches (one per tape) in parallel, coupled along length by an interface conductance. Each tape obeys E = Ec (I/Ic(θ,B,T))^n(θ,B,T) over the superconducting transition, extended with a normal bypass when quenched; the interface is modeled as a constant per-unit-length conductance Gc = 1/Rc.
- Implementation:
  - 1D distributed model solved using finite-difference along length L (Δx ≈ 1–2 mm) to capture current transfer length effects; boundary conditions reflect uniform current injection at ends.
  - Inputs: the measured Ic(θ) and n(θ) for each single tape; fit parameter: Rc (Ω·m⁻¹) or ρc (Ω·cm²) times width.
- Fitting:
  - Nonlinear least squares (Levenberg–Marquardt) minimizing the difference between measured and simulated V–I curves at θ = 0°, 45°, 90° to extract a single Rc explaining all three angles; validate by predicting V–I at other angles.
- Outputs:
  - Rc (and uncertainty), current partition versus I, predicted Ic,FFDS(θ) vs measured.

Section C. Feasibility Assessment

C1. Resources and facilities
- Reel-to-reel PLD with temperature and pO2 control; excimer laser 248 nm.
- IBAD-MgO/LMO buffered Hastelloy tapes from commercial suppliers.
- Reel-to-reel hot lamination/soldering line with temperature, pressure control in inert atmosphere.
- XRD (four-circle), SEM/AFM, TEM/STEM-EDS (collaboration or user facility).
- Cryogenic magnet system with rotator, 65–77 K capability, 1.5 T field, precision current source.

C2. Timeline (indicative, 9–12 months)
- Months 1–2: Substrate qualification; PLD parameter optimization on small coupons; baseline YBCO and EuBCO depositions.
- Months 3–4: EuBCO+BHO optimization; microstructure verification; texture mapping.
- Months 5–6: Single-tape transport measurements; finalize deposition recipes.
- Months 6–7: FFDS solder process development; contact resistivity coupons; produce target and control stacks.
- Months 8–9: Angular transport and I–V characterization; MO imaging.
- Months 9–10: Modeling and Rc extraction; ablation studies (texture, APC, interface).
- Months 11–12: Replication, statistics, and final analysis.

C3. Risks and mitigations
- Risk: Excessive BHO degrades Tc or ab-plane Jc.
  - Mitigation: Fix BHO at 3.5 mol%; verify Tc (onset > 88–90 K); cross-compare with 2.5 and 5 mol% in small runs to confirm optimum.
- Risk: Solder wets poorly or forms high Rc due to surface oxides.
  - Mitigation: Inert N2, Au flash metallization ablation, gentle Ar cleaning; strict handling to avoid air exposure prior to lamination.
- Risk: Δφ degradation along long lengths.
  - Mitigation: Continuous texture monitoring; restrict evaluation to sections with Δφ within spec; collaborate with substrate vendor for process control.
- Risk: Mechanical strain or thermal mismatch induces microcracks.
  - Mitigation: Thin solder (2–4 μm) at 200 °C; controlled cooling; bend-radius limits during handling; optional finite-element thermomechanical simulation.
- Risk: Model identifiability of Rc.
  - Mitigation: Use multiple angles and full I–V curves; cross-check with lap-joint ρc measurements.

Section D. Data Analysis and Result Evaluation

D1. Angular performance analysis
- Compute Ic(θ) for all samples; compare:
  - Single-tape anisotropy: σ(Ic)/⟨Ic⟩ and Ic,max/Ic,min for YBCO vs EuBCO+BHO.
  - FFDS-solder vs sum-of-individuals: quantify ΔIc(θ); acceptance if |ΔIc(θ)| ≤ 5% across angles (within experimental uncertainty).
  - FFDS-insulated control: expect Ic,FFDS ≈ max[Ic,YBCO(θ), Ic,EuBCO+BHO(θ)], not the sum.
  - FFDS-thick/oxidized: expect partial current sharing; evaluate reduction in anisotropy versus Rc.
- Report improvements: increase of Ic,min, reduction of σ(Ic)/⟨Ic⟩ from single tapes to FFDS.

D2. n-value and stability
- Compare n(θ) for single vs FFDS; ensure no systematic degradation; correlate any reduction with Rc or localized heating.

D3. Model validation
- Using single-tape Ic(θ), n(θ), fit Rc to FFDS V–I at three angles; predict at other angles and compare with measurements. Accept model if prediction error <10% for Ic across full angular sweep.
- Extract current partition at onset of flux flow to confirm efficient transfer from the first-quenched tape to its partner.

D4. Microstructure–property correlation
- Correlate BHO nanorod density/alignment (TEM) with c-axis Ic enhancement (θ ≈ 0°).
- Correlate Δφ with ab-plane performance (θ ≈ 90°) and overall anisotropy.

Section E. Potential Extensions (optional after primary goals)
- Higher field/temperature mapping (e.g., 3–5 T at 65 K; 77 K at 1–2 T) for application-relevant matrices.
- Short-coil subscale tests to evaluate winding-engineering current density Je and quench sharing, once straight-tape performance is validated.

Section F. References to Previous Studies (pre‑2025)
- Foltyn, S. R., et al., “Materials science challenges for high-temperature superconducting wire,” Nature Materials 6, 631–642 (2007). Review of coated conductor architectures, texture, and APC strategies.
- Iijima, Y., et al., “Biaxially aligned YBa2Cu3O7−x thin films on polycrystalline nickel tapes by ion beam assisted deposition,” Applied Physics Letters 60, 769–771 (1992). Foundational IBAD approach for textured templates.
- Goyal, A., et al., “High critical current density superconducting tapes by epitaxial deposition on biaxially textured templates,” Applied Physics Letters 69, 1795–1797 (1996). Early demonstration of high-Jc on textured substrates.
- MacManus-Driscoll, J. L., et al., “Strongly enhanced current densities in superconducting coated conductors of YBa2Cu3O7−x + BaZrO3,” Nature Materials 3, 439–443 (2004). Introduction of self-assembled nanocolumnar APCs in REBCO.
- Kang, S., et al., “High-performance high-Tc superconducting wires,” Science 311, 1911–1914 (2006). Demonstrated BaZrO3 nanorods and substantial Jc enhancement in high fields.
- Maiorov, B., et al., “Synergetic combination of different types of defect to optimize pinning in high-temperature superconductors,” Nature Materials 8, 398–404 (2009). Optimization of correlated and random pinning for angular performance.
- Miura, M., et al., “Enhancement of flux pinning by BaHfO3 nanorods in REBCO thin films,” Superconductor Science and Technology 26, 035008 (2013). Shows BaHfO3 nanorods as effective c-axis APCs in REBCO films.
- Hasegawa, T., et al., “LaMnO3 buffer layers for YBCO coated conductors,” Physica C 357–360, 1299–1302 (2001). Use of LMO as a chemically compatible cap/buffer promoting epitaxy.
- IEC 61788-13: “Superconductivity—Part 13: AC loss characterization and DC critical current measurement of HTS wires,” International Electrotechnical Commission (2013). Defines standardized critical current measurement methods.
- Takayasu, M., et al., “Low-resistance soldered joints of REBCO coated conductors,” IEEE Transactions on Applied Superconductivity 25, 6601805 (2015). Demonstrated sub‑10 nΩ·cm² contact resistivity in Sn/Pb soldered joints.
- Sumption, M. D., et al., “Characterization of electrical contact resistance of joints between coated conductors,” Superconductor Science and Technology 23, 045012 (2010). Methods and values for joint/contact resistance in REBCO tapes.
- Ekin, J. W., “Strain effects in superconductors,” in Experimental Techniques for Low-Temperature Measurements (Oxford Univ. Press, 2006), Ch. 11. Mechanical strain limits and considerations in superconductors.

Notes on Concepts Utilized
- Artificial pinning centers (APCs): Second-phase nanoinclusions (e.g., BHO) that self-assemble as c-axis aligned nanorods in REBCO during PLD, providing correlated pinning most effective when B//c, thereby enhancing Jc where undoped REBCO is weakest.
- In-plane texture Δφ: Full width at half maximum (FWHM) of in-plane orientation distribution measured by φ-scans; smaller Δφ indicates better grain alignment and reduced weak-link behavior.
- Equivalent-circuit current-sharing model: Represents each tape’s nonlinear E–I behavior and couples them via a resistive interface. A low Rc allows current to transfer from a tape entering flux flow to its partner, raising the stack’s Ic,min and reducing angular anisotropy.

End Criteria for Success
- Verified BHO nanorods in EuBCO by TEM with c-axis alignment.
- Single-tape Ic(θ) shows complementary maxima: YBCO strong near θ ≈ 90°, EuBCO+BHO strong near θ ≈ 0°.
- FFDS-solder achieves Ic,FFDS(θ) within ±5% of the arithmetic sum of single-tape Ic(θ) over the full angular range at 65 K, 1.5 T.
- Angular anisotropy reduced (e.g., σ(Ic)/⟨Ic⟩ halved relative to single tapes) with a significant increase in Ic,min.
- Extracted interface contact resistivity ρc in the range 1–5 nΩ·cm²; ablations show monotonic degradation of anisotropy reduction as Rc increases.

Step 1: Fabricate two 4 mm-wide precursor tapes  
 – YBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ (YBCO) CC without artificial pinning centres (APCs)  
 – EuBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ (EuBCO) CC doped with 3.5 mol % BaHfO₃ (BHO) as APCs  

Step 2: Deposit superconducting layers by pulsed-laser deposition (PLD)  
 – Substrate stack: LaMnO₃ (LMO) / IBAD-MgO / Y₂O₃ / Al₂O₃ / Hastelloy C-276

Step 3: Produce ~10 m long tapes of each type; slit to 4 mm width  

Step 4: Assemble FFDS conductor by reel-to-reel soldering  
 – Stack YBCO and EuBCO-BHO tapes face-to-face (superconducting sides inward)  
 – Solder alloy: Sn₆₃Pb₃₇ (T_flow = 183 °C)  
 – Bath temperature: ≈ 200 °C → final solder thickness 2–4 µm  

Step 5: Cut 60 mm long samples from the ends of each single tape and from the FFDS conductor for electrical testing  

Step 6: Mount samples in a rotatable cryostat probe  
 – Attach voltage taps on the top (EuBCO-BHO) side with 10 mm separation  
 – Apply current through the same top surface (four-probe arrangement, Fig. 3)  

Step 7: Perform I–V measurements  
 – Magnetic field: 1.5 T, temperature: 65 K  
 – Field angle θ swept from −40° to 220° in the plane perpendicular to the tape width  
 – Record I–V curves at θ = 0° (B || c-axis), 45°, 90° (B || a-b plane) and intermediate angles  

Step 8: Analyse data  
 – Extract critical current Ic (1 µV cm⁻¹ criterion) at each angle  
 – Fit FFDS I–V curves with an equivalent-circuit model: two nonlinear superconducting resistances R_sc(YBCO), R_sc(EuBCO) connected through a constant joint resistance R_c (fitted value 2 nΩ)  
 – Compare experimental Ic(θ) with the arithmetic sum Ic,YBCO(θ) + Ic,EuBCO(θ)  
 – Quantify anisotropy by standard deviation of Ic(θ) normalized to average Ic

- Sample geometry: 4 mm wide, 60 mm gauge length  
- Solder joint resistivity: ≈ 50 nΩ cm² at 77 K (cited from authors’ earlier work); fitted R_c = 2 nΩ for present 65 K data

Experiment:
Step1: Overview and objectives
- Goal: Quantitatively validate and optimize a substrate-induced vortex pinning strategy in pure YBa2Cu3O7−δ (YBCO) thin films using vertically aligned CeO2 nanorods embedded only in an SrTiO3 (STO) nanocomposite (NC) buffer on MgO(100). The hypothesis is that a high density of interfacial misfit and threading dislocations transferred from the NC buffer, together with controlled YBCO growth kinetics, creates c-axis–correlated pinning without degrading Tc or adding second phases inside YBCO. Target application space is coated conductors operating at T ≤ 40 K and μ0H ≥ 5 T.
- Key performance metrics and acceptance criteria:
  - Retention of Tc ≥ 89 K (onset, ±0.2 K) and self-field Jc(77 K) ≥ 2.0 MA cm−2.
  - Enhanced in-field performance: maximize Fp = μ0 H Jc at 20–40 K. Specific target: approach ≥ 600 GN m−3 at 20 K and 9 T in optimized samples.
  - Clear c-axis correlated pinning signature: pronounced Jc(θ) peak at B∥c with full-width at half maximum (FWHM) ≤ 8–12° at 20–40 K and ≥3 T.
  - Chemical purity of YBCO: below detection of Ce/Ti in YBCO layer by STEM-EDX and SIMS; no secondary phases in YBCO by XRD.

Step2: Experimental design—sample matrix, baselines, controls, and ablation studies
- Substrates: 10 × 10 × 0.5 mm3 MgO(100) single crystals ( epi-ready, rms roughness ≤ 0.3 nm).
- Buffers (100–150 nm total): 
  - Control buffer: epitaxial STO.
  - NC buffer: epitaxial STO + CeO2 vertically aligned nanocomposite (VAN) with CeO2 nanopillars.
  - Optional cap: 5–10 nm pure STO layer atop the NC to minimize any chemical exchange into YBCO.
- Superconductor: c-axis–oriented YBCO films, thickness 300–360 nm.
- Factorial design (minimum n = 3 independent wafers per condition for statistics):
  1) Buffer type (2 levels): pure STO vs STO+CeO2 NC (baseline comparison to isolate the interface effect).
  2) CeO2 volume fraction in NC (3 levels): 10, 20, 30 vol% (pins density tuning; expectation: more CeO2 → more STO/CeO2 interfaces → more threading dislocations).
  3) NC buffer thickness (2 levels): 100 and 150 nm (strain/dislocation injection tuning).
  4) YBCO laser repetition rate (4 levels): 10, 20, 50, 100 Hz (growth kinetics tuning; low frequency expected to yield straighter threading dislocations and stronger c-axis correlation).
  5) Additional controls: YBCO on single-crystal STO(001) (no MgO) at 20 and 100 Hz to benchmark frequency-driven Tc sensitivity without MgO-induced misfit.
- Ablation logic:
  - Remove CeO2 (use pure STO buffer) to quantify the incremental effect of the NC interfaces on dislocation density and pinning (interface tuning).
  - Fix buffer (NC with the best CeO2 fraction) and vary laser repetition rate to isolate growth-kinetics–induced straight vs wavy dislocation morphology (stress/growth tuning).
  - Fix repetition rate (20 Hz) and vary CeO2 fraction to map pinning vs dislocation density without changing defect morphology.
  - Fix repetition rate and CeO2 fraction, vary NC thickness to probe misfit/strain transfer strength.
- Statistical plan:
  - For each condition, characterize ≥ 3 bridges per wafer and ≥ 2 wafers per condition (effective N ≥ 6 bridges/condition).
  - Use ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey tests to establish significant differences in Jc and Fp; report means ± 1σ and 95% CI.
  - Power analysis (α = 0.05, power 0.8) indicates N ≥ 6 bridges detects ≥15% effect size assuming σ/μ ≈ 8–10%, typical for patterned YBCO bridges.

Step3: Process flow and critical parameters
- Substrate preparation:
  - Solvent clean (acetone, isopropanol), UV-ozone 15 min, anneal 800 °C in flowing O2 for 30 min to smooth surface terraces.
- Buffer deposition (PLD, KrF 248 nm):
  - Chamber base pressure ≤ 5 × 10−7 Torr; O2 pressure 400 mTorr; substrate temperature 870–890 °C (pyrometer).
  - Target–substrate distance 50–55 mm; laser fluence 1.5–2.0 J cm−2; repetition rate 10 Hz for both STO and NC buffer growth to promote vertical alignment.
  - NC buffer: alternate sub-monolayer bursts from STO and CeO2 targets or use a composite target if previously demonstrated to yield VANs; optimize plume sequence to achieve vertical CeO2 nanopillars (~tens of nm diameter, 10–20 nm lateral spacing). Grow to 100 or 150 nm.
  - Optional STO cap 5–10 nm at 10 Hz to stabilize the top surface chemistry.
  - Cool to 600 °C in 500 Torr O2, hold 20 min to reduce oxygen vacancies in buffer; then cool to room temperature.
- YBCO deposition (PLD, separate chamber preferred to avoid cross-contamination):
  - Base pressure ≤ 5 × 10−7 Torr; O2 pressure 250–300 mTorr; substrate temperature 780–800 °C; laser fluence 1.5–2.0 J cm−2.
  - Repetition rate as per design matrix (10, 20, 50, 100 Hz). Maintain constant total thickness (monitor by in situ plume counts and ex situ X-ray reflectivity for calibration).
  - Post-deposition oxygenation: ramp to 500 °C in 1 atm O2 within 5 min, hold 30–60 min, cool to room temperature at 5 °C min−1; optional final 350 °C oxygen anneal (1 atm) 2 h to maximize δ ≈ 0.07–0.10.
- Protective/contact layer and patterning:
  - In-situ Au cap 15–20 nm at 150–200 °C (sputter) to prevent surface degradation.
  - Photolithography and Ar ion milling to define micro-bridges 50 and 100 μm wide (length 200–500 μm). Protect Au pads for contacts; remove Au from the bridge center if necessary to avoid shunting; four-probe geometry with voltage taps 100–200 μm apart.

Step4: Structural, chemical, and microstructural characterization
- X-ray diffraction (Cu Kα1):
  - θ–2θ scans to confirm phase purity and c-axis orientation; rocking curves (ω) on YBCO(005), FWHM target ≤ 0.3–0.5°; φ scans on YBCO(103), STO(103), CeO2(220) to confirm cube-on-cube epitaxy with Δφ ≤ 3°.
  - Reciprocal space maps (RSMs) around YBCO(103/109) and buffer reflections to assess in-plane strain/relaxation and possible c-axis elongation; target: minimal c-axis elongation (<0.5%) to avoid Tc suppression.
- STEM and EDX:
  - Cross-sectional HAADF-STEM to image buffer VANs (CeO2 nanorods) and threading dislocations propagating into YBCO; measure dislocation areal density (μm−1) and straightness (quantify meander amplitude and correlation length).
  - Plan-view TEM on thinned samples to count threading dislocations per μm; apply g·b invisibility criteria to verify Burgers vectors.
  - EDX line scans and maps to verify no Ce/Ti penetration into YBCO above background; detection limit ≤ 0.2 at%.
  - Geometrical phase analysis (GPA) on STEM images to map local strain (εxx, εzz) near the interface and within YBCO; correlate strain fields with pinning performance.
- SIMS (optional, depth profiling):
  - Quantify Ce, Ti, Sr profiles; confirm a sharp chemical interface between buffer and YBCO.

Step5: Electrical transport and magneto-transport measurements
- Resistivity and Tc:
  - ρ(T) from 300 K to 10 K at zero field; define Tc, onset and zero; target ≥ 89 K onset with narrow transition (<0.8 K).
- Critical current density Jc(H,T,θ):
  - Four-probe transport in PPMS (0–9 T) at 20, 30, 40, 65, and 77 K; 1 μV cm−1 criterion.
  - Fields up to 9 T; angular Jc(θ) at fixed fields (e.g., 3, 5, 7, 9 T) with 0° = B∥c. Step θ by 2–5°; record full 0–180° scans.
- Derived quantities:
  - Fp(H,T) = μ0 H Jc(H,T); determine Fp,max(T) and field position of peak Hmax(T).
  - Irreversibility field Hirr(T) by Kramer extrapolation or Jc threshold (e.g., 1×102 A cm−2); construct reduced pinning curves f(h)=Fp/Fp,max vs h=H/Hirr for mechanism analysis.

Step6: Data analysis and result evaluation
- Mechanism identification:
  - Fit f(h) with Dew-Hughes scaling f(h) ∝ h^p (1 − h)^q; point defects typically p≈0.5, q≈2; surface/correlated pins shift Hmax to higher h and alter p,q. A higher Hmax/Hirr and narrow c-axis peak in Jc(θ) indicate strong correlated pinning.
  - Kramer plots [Jc^0.5 H^0.25 vs H] to extrapolate Hirr and compare across samples.
  - Anisotropy analysis with Blatter’s scaling: collapse Jc(θ) using effective field Heff = H√(cos2θ + γ−2 sin2θ) to obtain mass anisotropy γ (~5–7 in YBCO at low T); deviations near B∥c quantify correlated pin contribution.
- Morphology–property correlations:
  - Correlate threading dislocation density and straightness metrics from STEM with Jc(θ=0°), Fp,max, and Hmax/Hirr. Hypothesis: straighter, denser threading dislocations increase B∥c peak amplitude and shift Hmax upward.
  - Compare NC vs STO buffers at fixed repetition rate: higher dislocation density with NC should raise Fp and strengthen c-axis peak without worsening Δφ or Tc.
  - Compare 20 Hz vs 100 Hz for same buffer: increased meandering at high frequency should broaden and weaken c-axis peak and lower Fp, particularly at 20–40 K and ≥3 T.
- Statistical validation:
  - Use ANOVA to test main effects (buffer type, repetition rate, CeO2 fraction) and interactions on Fp,max(20–40 K) and Jc(θ=0°, 3–9 T).
  - Report effect sizes (Cohen’s d) and Pearson/Spearman correlations between microstructural metrics and transport performance.
- Success criteria:
  - Demonstrate statistically significant (p < 0.05) enhancement of Fp,max and Jc(B∥c) with NC buffer over pure STO at matched thickness and repetition rate, with Tc and self-field Jc unchanged within ±5%.
  - Establish an optimal deposition frequency window (10–20 Hz) which maximizes c-axis correlated pinning without texture degradation.

Step7: Implementation details—technologies and methodologies
- VAN buffer growth (STO+CeO2):
  - Concept: Large lattice mismatch (e.g., CeO2/MgO ~ 26%, STO/MgO ~ 7–8%) drives vertical phase separation during PLD under kinetically limited growth, forming CeO2 nanopillars within an STO matrix. The high density of vertical STO/CeO2 interfaces creates an interfacial misfit network at the top of the buffer that injects threading dislocations into the overlying YBCO.
  - Implementation routes:
    - Alternating-target PLD: Cycle 5–20 pulses on STO and 1–3 pulses on CeO2 to tune CeO2 volume fraction; maintain 10 Hz and high substrate temperature (≈880 °C) to encourage vertical alignment rather than lateral clustering.
    - Composite target PLD: Single target with pre-mixed STO–CeO2 (10–30 vol% CeO2). Validate VAN formation by STEM.
  - Key controls: Maintain oxygen pressure high enough (≈400 mTorr) to suppress oxygen vacancies that could relax strain; limit total layer thickness to prevent buckling/relaxation; include a thin STO cap to stabilize the surface chemistry for YBCO nucleation.
- YBCO growth kinetics control:
  - Principle: Lower repetition rate increases terrace adatom diffusion time between pulses, favoring layer-by-layer growth and straight threading dislocations. Higher rate increases instantaneous flux and roughness, promoting meandering of dislocations and sub-grain mosaicity.
  - Practical control: Use identical laser fluence, substrate temperature, and oxygen pressure; only change repetition rate. Calibrate thickness per 1000 pulses at each rate to maintain constant film thickness.
- Microfabrication and contacts:
  - Au capping protects from ambient; sputtered Au contact pads serve as low-resistance leads. Use low-temperature cure resists to avoid oxygen loss. Ion milling minimizes chemical contamination.
- Microscopy and strain mapping:
  - Prepare electron-transparent lamellae by FIB with low-kV final polish to reduce damage. Use HAADF-STEM for Z-contrast to clearly distinguish CeO2 vs STO and YBCO. Apply GPA on atomic-resolution images to obtain local strain; correlate with dislocation cores and YBCO lattice.
- Transport measurement fidelity:
  - Use four-probe configuration with minimal contact resistance; verify linear V–I above noise. Apply voltage criterion 1 μV cm−1. Thermal stabilize sample at each T for ≥10 min. For angular measurements, ensure misalignment < 0.5° using Hall probe or platform calibration. Correct for self-field effects at low H where necessary.

Step8: Feasibility, resources, and timeline
- Equipment and availability:
  - Two-chamber PLD with KrF excimer laser and multi-target carousel; substrate heater up to 900 °C; O2 up to 1 atm; optional in-situ RHEED for growth monitoring.
  - XRD with RSM capability; aberration-corrected STEM with EDX; FIB for TEM lamellae; SIMS depth profiling; PPMS (9 T) with rotator and low-T option (down to 10 K).
- Personnel:
  - 1 thin-film growth expert (PLD), 1 microscopy specialist (STEM/GPA), 1 device/transport physicist, 1 XRD/strain analyst, and 1 data/statistics lead. Shared technician support for microfabrication and PPMS scheduling.
- Throughput and time estimate (Phase I, optimization and validation, 6 months):
  - Months 0–1: Buffer growth calibration (STO and NC), VAN confirmation by STEM for 2–3 compositions.
  - Months 1–3: YBCO growth across repetition rates (10, 20, 50, 100 Hz) on STO and NC buffers; initial XRD and Tc/Jc screening; down-select best CeO2 fraction and buffer thickness.
  - Months 3–5: Full microscopy and SIMS on down-selected conditions; full PPMS mapping Jc(H,T,θ).
  - Months 5–6: Data analysis, Dew-Hughes/Kramer/anisotropy fits; write-up and iteration plan.
- Risks and mitigation:
  - Risk: Ce/Ti diffusion into YBCO. Mitigation: thin STO cap; keep YBCO growth temperature ≤ 800 °C; verify with EDX/SIMS.
  - Risk: VAN misalignment (non-vertical rods). Mitigation: tune substrate temperature/oxygen pressure and pulse sequencing; confirm early with STEM.
  - Risk: Texture degradation at high repetition rates. Mitigation: maintain Δφ ≤ 3° by adjusting temperature and oxygen; if needed, reduce rate or increase relaxation time between bursts (burst mode with pauses).
  - Risk: Oxygenation nonuniformity affecting Tc/Jc. Mitigation: standardized post-anneal, verify δ by ρ(300 K)/ρ(100 K) ratios and Tc shape; iterate anneal times.
- Scalability:
  - The approach is compatible with long-length coated conductors using IBAD-MgO templates: the NC buffer concept can be applied atop IBAD MgO/LaMnO3 or Gd2Zr2O7 cap layers. Follow-on tests on short IBAD coupons are recommended after Phase I.

Step9: Expected outcomes and decision points
- Expectation: NC buffers increase threading dislocation density in YBCO (10–20 μm−1) and induce local strain, boosting correlated pinning along c. Low-frequency (10–20 Hz) YBCO growth yields straighter dislocations and higher Fp than high-frequency (100 Hz) growth.
- Decision metrics:
  - If NC buffer + 20 Hz achieves ≥ 30% higher Fp,max at 20–40 K vs pure STO buffer and maintains Tc/self-field Jc within ±5%, proceed to IBAD-MgO templates.
  - If CeO2 fraction > 20% degrades texture or Tc, cap at 10–20% and focus on repetition rate optimization.
  - If high-frequency growth compromises Δφ or induces wavy dislocations, restrict production window to ≤ 20 Hz for high-field, low-T applications.

Step10: References to previous studies (pre-2025)
- Dew-Hughes, D., Flux pinning mechanisms in type II superconductors, Philosophical Magazine 30, 293–305 (1974). Classic framework for f(h) scaling and pinning classifications.
- Blatter, G., Feigel’man, M. V., Geshkenbein, V. B., Larkin, A. I., Vinokur, V. M., Vortices in high-temperature superconductors, Reviews of Modern Physics 66, 1125–1388 (1994). Anisotropic scaling and vortex physics in cuprates.
- Civale, L., et al., Vortex confinement by columnar defects in YBa2Cu3O7 crystals, Physical Review Letters 67, 648–651 (1991). Benchmark for c-axis–correlated pinning and angular Jc signatures.
- Dam, B., et al., Origin of high critical currents in YBa2Cu3O7−δ thin films, Nature 399, 439–442 (1999). Demonstrates strong pinning by dislocations in YBCO thin films.
- Foltyn, S. R., et al., Materials science challenges for high-temperature superconducting wire, Nature Materials 6, 631–642 (2007). Overview of coated conductor microstructure and pinning.
- MacManus-Driscoll, J. L., et al., Strongly enhanced current densities in superconducting coated conductors made by self-assembly, Nature Materials 3, 439–443 (2004). Self-assembled vertical pins (e.g., BaZrO3) within YBCO as a comparator to substrate-induced strategies.
- Gutiérrez, J., et al., Strong isotropic flux pinning in solution-derived YBa2Cu3O7−x nanocomposite films, Nature Materials 6, 367–373 (2007). Nanocomposite strategies and f(h) behavior.
- Maiorov, B., et al., Synergetic combination of different types of defect to optimize pinning in high-Tc superconductors, Nature Materials 8, 398–404 (2009). Interplay of defect types and low-T/high-H optimization.
- Kramer, E. J., Scaling laws for flux pinning in hard superconductors, Journal of Applied Physics 44, 1360–1370 (1973). Kramer plot analysis for determining Hirr.
- Venables, J. A., Spiller, G. D. T., Hanbücken, M., Nucleation and growth of thin films, Reports on Progress in Physics 47, 399–459 (1984). Growth kinetics, adatom diffusion, and the impact of deposition rate on film morphology.
- MacManus-Driscoll, J. L., et al., Functional oxide nanocomposite thin films, MRS Bulletin 35, 614–622 (2010). Design principles and growth of vertically aligned nanocomposites (VANs) in oxides, including STO-based systems.
- Chen, A., and MacManus-Driscoll, J. L., Self-assembled epitaxial oxide nanocomposite thin films: structure, properties and growth mechanisms, Materials Science and Engineering R 67, 249–265 (2010). VAN growth mechanisms and strain/interface control in perovskite–fluorite systems relevant to STO–CeO2.

[Experimental Workflow]
Step 1: Substrate preparation  
- Start with commercial MgO(100) single-crystal substrates (no further surface treatment described).

Step 2: Buffer-layer deposition (separate PLD chamber)  
- Deposit 100–150 nm STO or STO+CeO₂ nanocomposite (NC) films by pulsed-laser deposition (PLD) using a KrF excimer laser (λ = 248 nm).  
  – Substrate temperature: 880 °C  
  – Laser repetition rate: 10 Hz  
  – Oxygen partial pressure: 400 mTorr  

Step 3: YBCO film deposition (different PLD chamber)  
- Deposit 300–360 nm YBCO on the buffered MgO.  
  – Substrate temperature: 890 °C  
  – Oxygen partial pressure: 400 mTorr  
  – Laser repetition rate: systematically varied (10, 20, 100 Hz; other frequencies not reported).  

Step 4: Micro-patterning for transport measurements  
- Cut micro-bridges (50–100 µm wide, 1 mm long) into the YBCO films using a UV laser cutter (λ = 355 nm).

Step 5: Structural characterization  
- X-ray diffraction: 2θ/ω and φ scans of MgO 202, STO 202, CeO₂ 202 reflections to verify epitaxy and texture.  
- Cross-sectional scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) for microstructure and elemental mapping.

Step 6: Superconducting property measurements  
- Mount samples in a Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS).  
- Perform four-probe DC transport:  
  – Measure resistive transition to obtain Tc (onset/offset criteria not specified).  
  – Record current–voltage curves at 77 K, 65 K, 40 K, 20 K in magnetic fields 0–9 T (field direction perpendicular to film surface unless otherwise noted).  
  – Define Jc with 1 µV cm⁻¹ electric-field criterion.  
- Extract flux-pinning force density Fp = Jc × B from the Jc(B) data.  
- Measure Jc(θ) at 65 K, 3 T and 40 K, 5 T by rotating the sample in a fixed magnetic field.

[Experimental Design Details]
- Buffer vs. reference: YBCO on bare STO single crystal (no buffer) served as a control.  
- Deposition-frequency matrix: Each buffer type (STO, NC) and the control were measured at multiple YBCO laser frequencies (10, 20, 100 Hz).  
- Temperature–field window: 77 K (0–9 T), 65 K (0–9 T), 40 K (0–9 T), 20 K (0–9 T).  
- Angular study: θ range and step size not specified; only representative curves at 65 K, 3 T and 40 K, 5 T are shown.

Title: Uniform transverse Jc in long-length EuBa2Cu3O7−δ (EuBCO) coated conductors with BaHfO3 nanocolumns by mitigating edge overheating, segregation, and interface degradation in reel‑to‑reel MPMT‑PLD

Hypotheses and Targets
- Hypothesis H1 (composition tuning): Edge overheating during helical travel in reel‑to‑reel MPMT‑PLD drives Cu segregation and Cu‑rich precipitates at edges, reducing local Jc; homogenizing the transverse temperature profile (ΔTwidth ≤ 5–10 °C at the growth zone) will suppress segregation and recover edge Jc to ≥95–100% of center.
- Hypothesis H2 (grain boundary/texture tuning): Buffer-layer volumetric changes and partial decomposition at edges under local thermal/chemical excursions produce arched, non‑c‑axis grains and higher angle boundaries; maintaining the buffer/EuBCO interface and in‑plane texture prevents arched grains and removes weak‑link paths, recovering ~25–30% Jc loss at edges.
- Hypothesis H3 (interface tuning): Maintaining stable CeO2 and LaMnO3 (LMO) buffers by keeping substrate temperature and oxygen potential within stability windows preserves a flat, epitaxial template and maintains BHO nanocolumn alignment.
- Hypothesis H4 (stress tuning): Reducing torsional stress and friction between tape edges and built‑up coating residue prevents localized hot spots and Ni contamination that catalyze buffer/EuBCO decomposition.
- Target outcome: Je (77 K, self‑field) ≥ 2.5×10^9 A m^−2 across 10 mm width with ≤5% transverse variation on ≥200 m lengths; transverse Jc at left/right edges ≥95% of center. Maintain BHO nanocolumn alignment and c‑axis texture uniformity.

Experimental Design

Overview and Baseline
- Baseline line and process: Use existing industrial reel‑to‑reel multi‑plume multi‑turn PLD (MPMT‑PLD) system with helical travel. Substrate: C276 tape with Al2O3 (~100 nm)/Y2O3 (~100 nm)/IBAD‑MgO (10–15 nm, Δφ 6–8°)/LaMnO3 (LMO, 50–100 nm)/CeO2 (30–50 nm) buffer stack. EuBCO target stoichiometry Eu:Ba:Cu ≈1:2:3. BHO doping 6–8 vol% via composite target or alternating PLD of BaHfO3. Total EuBCO thickness 0.8–1.2 μm. Typical PLD conditions: KrF 248 nm, 3–10 J cm^−2 fluence, 5–20 Hz per plume, PO2 = 200–300 mTorr, growth temperature 770–800 °C, O2 flow 0.5–1 slm, growth rate 1–2 nm s^−1. Post‑growth oxygenation: cool to 450 °C in 400–600 Torr O2, hold 30–60 min, then cool to ambient.
- Baseline metrics: Transverse Jc mapping by slitting into 1–2 mm filaments and four‑probe Ic at 77 K, self‑field (1 μV cm^−1). Magnetization‑based Ic via VSM with Bean model for cross‑check. Micro‑XRD with 50 μm beam for (005) intensity and Δφ across width. SEM‑EDS line scans for Ba/Cu/Eu; FIB‑TEM/EDS for BHO nanorods, arched grains, Cu‑rich precipitates; ICP‑OES on edge/center sections for average stoichiometry. In‑situ transverse temperature mapping by two‑color pyrometry at left/mid/right and IR imaging through viewport on dummy runs.
- Expected baseline outcome: Edge Jc ~70–80% of center; micro‑XRD shows suppressed (005) at edges; TEM shows arched grains and Cu‑rich precipitates near edges; signs of incipient CeO2/LMO degradation at extreme edges.

Factor Space and Comparative Plan
- Factor A: Transverse temperature homogenization
  - A0: Existing unsegmented heater, no edge shielding, standard gas flow.
  - A1: Segmented backside heater (left/center/right zones) with closed‑loop feedback to multi‑spot pyrometry; polished Mo edge radiation shields; symmetric, widened O2 flow manifold and flow straighteners to equalize convective cooling/heating; refined helical pitch to equalize edge dwell time per turn; laser plume power redistribution across width to minimize center‑bias heating.
- Factor B: Interface stability and oxygen potential control
  - B0: Standard setpoint PO2 and ramp profile.
  - B1: Higher PO2 at growth edge of zone (250–350 mTorr) with rapid PO2 recovery during tape idling; controlled cool‑down with pO2 ≥400 Torr through 500–450 °C; minimize time above 820 °C equivalent at any transverse location; optional pre‑coat of 2–5 nm CeO2 densification layer by PLD at high PO2 prior to EuBCO to suppress surface oxygen vacancy formation.
- Factor C: Mechanical stress and edge‑friction mitigation
  - C0: Standard roller geometry and tension.
  - C1: Low‑runout crowned rollers with Ra<0.05 μm; web tension 20–30 N with twist <1°/100 mm; edge clearance baffles to prevent contact with built‑up coating in inter‑lane gaps; periodic in‑vacuo residue removal on shrouds/fixtures; redesign of entry/exit guide angle to reduce torsional component at the growth zone; no contact with coated surface in hot zone.
- Factor D: Composition control
  - D0: Single EuBCO+BHO composite target.
  - D1: Slight Ba‑rich (≤1–2 at.%) EuBCO target tuning to counter edge Cu enrichment when any residual ΔT remains; optional multi‑plume composition leveling: add a dedicated Ba‑rich microplume at edges to compensate for any measured edge deficiency; verify no secondary phases form.
- Factor E: BHO nanocolumn robustness
  - E0: Reference BHO content 0 vol%.
  - E1: BHO content 6–8 vol%. Keep other factors constant to test that interventions do not degrade nanorod alignment, density, and in‑field Jc.

Design of Experiments (DoE), Controls, and Ablations
- Phase I (diagnostics): A0–B0–C0–D0/E0 (undoped baseline) vs A0–B0–C0–D0/E1 (BHO‑doped baseline) on 50 m tapes to establish starting transverse ΔT, texture, segregation, arched grains, and Jc profile; quantify plume thickness distribution and thermal map.
- Phase II (single‑factor improvements): Apply A1 only; A1–B0–C0–D0/E1. Repeat on 100 m. Measure ΔTwidth and changes in Cu‑segregation and edge Jc. Then B1 only; A0–B1–C0–D0/E1. Then C1 only; A0–B0–C1–D0/E1. Then D1 only; A0–B0–C0–D1/E1. Each on ≥50 m.
- Phase III (factor combinations): Implement combined A1+B1, A1+C1, B1+C1, and A1+B1+C1 with D0/E1. Two repeats each on ≥200 m to assess reproducibility and interactions (2^k reduced factorial with replication). Include one arm with E0 (no BHO) under optimum A1+B1+C1 to check if improvements are independent of pinning landscape.
- Phase IV (robustness and scale): Best configuration on ≥500 m; sample at every 20 m (center + 1 mm from each edge); perform full transverse mapping on three segments (start/middle/end).

Evaluation Criteria and Statistical Analysis
- Thermal uniformity: ΔTwidth ≤ 5–10 °C at the growth zone measured by three‑spot two‑color pyrometry, confirmed by IR imaging on dummy runs; acceptance if ΔTwidth reduction ≥70% versus baseline.
- Composition: SEM‑EDS and ICP‑OES show Ba/Cu within ±2% across width; Cu‑rich precipitate area fraction at edges <0.5% by image analysis; edge‑to‑center EDS Cu count ratio 0.98–1.02.
- Texture and grains: Micro‑XRD (005) intensity variation across width ≤10%; Δφ of EuBCO and CeO2 ≤1° change from center to edge; TEM shows vertical BHO nanorods (4–8 nm diameter, 10–20 nm spacing), <5° tilt distribution uniform across width; arched non‑c‑axis grains at edges eliminated (<1% area).
- Electrical: Edge Jc ≥95% of center value (goal ~100%); Je ≥2.5×10^9 A m^−2 with ≤5% transverse variation at 77 K, self‑field; magnetization‑derived Ic agrees with transport within ±5%.
- Statistics: For Phase II/III, use ANOVA on the response “edge/center Jc ratio” and “ΔTwidth” to quantify factor effects and interactions (α=0.05). Report means ±1σ and 95% confidence intervals. Use Pearson/Spearman correlation between ΔTwidth, Cu‑segregation, arched grain fraction, and edge Jc to establish causal links.

Implementation of Technologies/Methods

Reel‑to‑Reel MPMT‑PLD Hardware and Process Control
- Segmented heater retrofit (A1): Replace monolithic backside radiant heater with three independently powered zones (left/center/right) using SiC or graphite elements behind a molybdenum heat spreader. Integrate three two‑color pyrometers (λ1~1.5 μm, λ2~1.0 μm) aimed at left edge (~1 mm in), center, and right edge; calibrate emissivity using a blackbody‑painted calibration coupon. Implement PID control per zone to maintain setpoint 780±3 °C, with adaptive setpoint offsets of up to ±15 °C to null measured ΔTwidth caused by helical travel.
- Edge radiation shields (A1): Install highly polished Mo or W side baffles at adjustable proximity (2–4 mm from tape edges) to equalize radiative boundary conditions and reduce edge heat loss/accretion. Ensure baffles do not intercept plume deposition; angle to avoid redeposition back onto the tape.
- Gas flow equalization (A1): Re‑design oxygen inlet to a plenum with flow straighteners (honeycomb) to supply laminar, symmetric flow across width. Verify with smoke‑wire or CFD prior to installation. Maintain PO2 250–300 mTorr; total flow 0.7–1.0 slm; monitor pO2 with capacitance manometer near the growth zone.
- Helical pitch and plume balancing (A1): Adjust tape wrap angle and pitch so that the integrated dwell and view factor of edges vs center per turn is equalized. Redistribute laser energy: edge plumes run +5–10% fluence, center −5% if thickness mapping shows center‑bias (verify by profilometry after short runs). Keep net thickness variation ≤5% across width.
- Interface oxygenation (B1): During transient holds (e.g., splices), boost PO2 to 400–500 mTorr to avoid buffer reduction. Implement a high‑PO2 “pre‑pulse” (10–20 s) prior to EuBCO deposition when the tape segment enters the plume to replenish oxygen in CeO2/LMO surface. Ensure cool‑down through 500–450 °C is conducted in ≥400 Torr O2 to complete EuBCO oxygenation and avoid oxygen vacancy formation in buffers.
- Stress and friction control (C1): Align all rollers to <50 μrad; employ crowned rollers with low roughness; set web tension 20–30 N; reduce twist angle at the hot zone to near zero by symmetric guide design; implement weekly in‑vacuo cleaning protocol for shrouds and inter‑lane gaps to prevent residue build‑up that can contact edges; avoid any edge contact hardware in the hot zone.
- Composition and BHO delivery (D1/E1):
  - Composite target method: EuBCO target with 6–8 vol% BHO uniformly dispersed; maintain laser fluence 3–5 J cm^−2 to avoid preferential ablation of Hf‑rich phases.
  - Alternating‑plume method: One plume ablates EuBCO, a second ablates BaHfO3, synchronized to yield net 6–8 vol% BHO; cycle ratio e.g., 9 pulses EuBCO:1 pulse BHO; adjust based on film stoichiometry by ICP‑OES.
  - Edge composition leveling: If residual edge Cu‑rich signatures persist, employ a slight Ba‑rich EuBCO target (Ba excess 1 at.%) or allocate an edge microplume delivering a Ba‑rich flux to restore Ba/Cu uniformity; validate that no Ba‑Cu‑O second phases appear by XRD.
- Post‑deposition oxygenation: After growth, ramp at 10–20 °C min^−1 to 450 °C in 400–600 Torr O2, hold 30–60 min, then cool at 10 °C min^−1 to room temperature. This avoids oxygen deficiency that can depress Jc and destabilize the CeO2/LMO interface.

Characterization and Metrology
- In‑situ transverse temperature mapping: Two‑color pyrometers with real‑time logging; cross‑validate with IR camera viewing surrogate runs using a calibrated emissivity coating on a dummy tape; record ΔTwidth statistics over 10 min windows per run.
- Thickness and morphology: Stylus profilometry across width every 5 mm on short “witness” coupons; AFM for surface roughness; ensure thickness uniformity within ≤5%.
- Microstructure: SEM‑BSE and EDS across the 10 mm width; quantify precipitate area fraction at 1 mm from each edge vs center. FIB‑TEM on lamellae from edge (0.5–1 mm in) and center: measure BHO nanorod diameter, spacing, and angular distribution; identify arched/non‑c‑axis grains; EELS mapping for Ni at the interface to detect contamination.
- Texture: Micro‑XRD (lab microfocus beam ~50 μm) mapping of EuBCO (005) intensity and rocking curves across width at 2–3 m intervals along length; φ‑scans for in‑plane texture of EuBCO and CeO2 at edge vs center.
- Composition: ICP‑OES on dissolved sections from edge and center for Eu, Ba, Cu (3 repeats) to quantify stoichiometry; SEM‑EDS line scans for Ba/Cu ratio uniformity within ±2%.
- Electrical transport: Slit the 10 mm tape into 1–2 mm filaments using a dicer or mechanical slitter; pattern 4‑probe contacts (Cu pads) at 10 cm intervals; measure Ic at 77 K, self‑field with 1 μV cm^−1 criterion per IEC 61788‑6; compute Jc for each filament; compute edge/center Jc ratios and transverse variation. Supplement with VSM magnetization measurements to extract Ic by Bean model; compare transport vs magnetization within ±5%.
- In‑field tests (sanity check): Measure Jc(H, θ) at 77 K up to 3 T for center and edges to ensure BHO nanocolumn pinning is preserved (peak near H∥c, angular bandwidth consistent with nanorods).

Feasibility Assessment

Resources and Timeline
- Existing R2R MPMT‑PLD line with capability for multi‑plume and helical travel; machine shop support to retrofit heater segmentation and edge shields; metrology suite with SEM‑EDS, FIB‑TEM, micro‑XRD, ICP‑OES, VSM, 77 K transport station.
- Personnel: 1 process engineer (PLD hardware and control), 1 thin film scientist (process recipes), 1 materials microscopist (SEM/TEM), 1 crystallographer (XRD), 1 test engineer (transport), 1 technician (tape handling and slitting).
- Timeline (12 months):
  - Months 1–3: Design/install segmented heater, edge shields, gas manifold; calibrate pyrometers and IR imaging; baseline runs (Phase I).
  - Months 4–6: Phase II single‑factor experiments and analysis; iterate setpoints to reach ΔTwidth ≤10 °C.
  - Months 7–9: Phase III factorial combinations; converge to A1+B1+C1 optimum; verify no adverse effect on BHO alignment.
  - Months 10–12: Phase IV long runs and reliability; document SOPs and control charts.

Risk and Mitigation
- Risk: Segmented heating may change thickness profile. Mitigation: Laser plume power redistribution and minor tape path adjustments; closed‑loop thickness monitoring with witness coupons.
- Risk: Edge shields could collect redeposited material. Mitigation: Polished, heated shields to reduce sticking; regular cleaning schedule; shield geometry to eliminate back‑sputtering onto tape.
- Risk: Increased PO2 could alter plume dynamics or roughness. Mitigation: Optimize fluence and target‑to‑substrate distance; maintain growth temperature; monitor roughness via AFM.
- Risk: BHO nanorod misalignment due to parameter changes. Mitigation: Keep T, PO2, and growth rate within known windows for vertical nanorod self‑assembly; verify by TEM after each change and revert if necessary.
- Risk: Sensor drift at high temperature. Mitigation: Weekly calibration of pyrometers against a reference blackbody; redundant sensors at center.

Step‑by‑Step Execution Plan

Experiment: Step 1: Establish Baseline
- Deposit EuBCO with 6–8 vol% BHO under baseline A0–B0–C0–D0/E1 on 50–100 m tape. Record in‑situ ΔTwidth; collect micro‑XRD maps, SEM‑EDS, FIB‑TEM at edges/center; perform transverse Jc mapping by slitting. Quantify edge/center Jc, Cu‑segregation, arched grain fraction, and any Ni at the interface.

Step 2: Implement Transverse Temperature Homogenization (A1)
- Retrofit segmented heaters and edge shields; balance gas flow and adjust helical pitch. Run two 100 m tapes at A1–B0–C0–D0/E1. Measure ΔTwidth reduction; repeat microstructure and electrical mapping. Acceptance: ΔTwidth ≤10 °C and ≥50% reduction in Cu‑rich precipitates at edges; ≥10% absolute improvement in edge/center Jc.

Step 3: Stabilize Interfaces and Oxygen Potential (B1)
- With A0, implement B1 PO2 protocols; deposit two 50 m tapes A0–B1–C0–D0/E1; assess CeO2/LMO integrity by TEM/EELS and micro‑XRD Δφ across width; check for reduced arched grains. Acceptance: No observable CeO2/LMO decomposition at edges; ≤1% arched grain area; ≥5% absolute improvement in edge/center Jc.

Step 4: Reduce Mechanical Stress and Edge Friction (C1)
- Install low‑runout crowned rollers, re‑align guides, clean shrouds, set tension/twist limits. Deposit two 50 m tapes A0–B0–C1–D0/E1; measure for Ni contamination at edges by EDS/EELS and hot spot incidence by IR imaging on dummy. Acceptance: No detectable Ni at interface; elimination of transient hot spots; ≥5% edge/center Jc improvement if mechanical overheating contributed.

Step 5: Composition Fine‑Tuning (D1) if needed
- If residual edge Cu‑enrichment remains, run two 50 m tapes A0–B0–C0–D1/E1; verify Ba/Cu uniformity by EDS/ICP; confirm no secondary phases; measure Jc uniformity. Acceptance: Ba/Cu ±2% across width; no new second phases; ≥5% improvement in edge/center Jc.

Step 6: Factor Combinations and Optimization (Phase III)
- Execute A1+B1, A1+C1, B1+C1 on ≥200 m tapes; finally A1+B1+C1; for each, repeat full metrology and transport mapping. Use ANOVA to quantify factor contributions. Select the best performing combination based on Jc uniformity and microstructure quality.

Step 7: BHO Robustness Check (E0 vs E1)
- Under the optimum A1+B1+C1, deposit two 50 m tapes without BHO (E0) and compare to with BHO (E1) to ensure process changes do not degrade nanocolumn alignment or c‑axis texture. Verify BHO nanorods remain vertical and uniformly distributed across width when present.

Step 8: Long‑Length Validation (Phase IV)
- Run ≥500 m with optimum A1+B1+C1 and D0 or D1 as required, with E1. Sample segments at 0, 250, 500 m; perform full transverse mapping and microstructure checks. Confirm Je ≥2.5×10^9 A m^−2 across width with ≤5% variation; edge/center Jc ≥95–100%. Document control setpoints and monitoring protocols.

Data Analysis and Interpretation
- Compile ΔTwidth vs edge/center Jc across all runs; compute correlation coefficients and fit linear models to establish thermal‑segregation‑Jc relationships. Plot arched grain fraction vs Jc loss to quantify microstructural contributions. Use Tukey’s HSD post‑hoc analysis after ANOVA to rank factors. Cross‑validate Ic from transport and Bean‑model magnetization within ±5%; investigate deviations.

Step 1: Tape fabrication  
- A several-hundred-metre-long, 10 mm-wide EuBCO tape with the layer sequence C276/Al2O3/Y2O3/IBAD-MgO/LaMnO3/CeO2/EuBCO/Ag (total thickness 54 µm) was grown on a Hastelloy C276 substrate using an industrial reel-to-reel MPMT-PLD system (details of deposition temperature, laser energy, repetition rate, oxygen pressure, tape speed, etc. are not given).

Step 2: Mechanical slitting  
- Two short sections were cut from the long tape.  
- Scheme 1: slit into five 2 mm-wide filaments.  
- Scheme 2: slit into six filaments (1/2/2/2/2/1 mm).  
(Exact slitting tool or conditions are not specified.)

Step 3: Transport Jc measurement (four-probe)  
- Each filament was measured at 77 K in self-field.  
- Critical current Ic was defined with a 1 µV cm⁻¹ electric-field criterion and extracted by power-law fitting.  
- Jc was calculated by dividing Ic by the filament cross-sectional area (thickness × width).

Step 4: Magnetic Jc measurement (Bean model)  
- For scheme-1 filaments, magnetic moment versus field (B || c-axis) was recorded at 77 K in a 9 T Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS).  
- Jc(μ₀H) was derived from the magnetic hysteresis loops using the Bean model.

Step 5: Chemical analysis  
- The silver cap layer was removed with an ammonia + hydrogen-peroxide solution.  
- Filaments from scheme 2 were dissolved and analysed with a Perkin-Elmer Avio™ 500 inductively-coupled-plasma optical-emission spectrometer (ICP-OES) to obtain Eu/Ba and Ba/Cu atomic ratios across the tape width.

Step 6: Surface morphology and local chemistry  
- A TESCAN RISE-MAGNA scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) was used to image the EuBCO surface and map elemental distributions.

Step 7: Crystallographic survey  
- Micro-area X-ray diffraction (micro-XRD) θ–2θ scans were performed with a Rigaku SmartLab system using a 50 µm-diameter Cu-Kα beam (λ = 1.54 Å).  
- Patterns were collected every 0.5 mm from the left edge to the centre (11 points total).  
- EuBCO (005) peak intensity was normalised to the CeO2 (002) peak to track relative crystallinity.

Step 8: Cross-sectional microstructure  
- A GAIA3 dual-beam focused-ion-beam (FIB) system prepared electron-transparent lamellae.  
- A Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM) with EDS mapped phase distribution, grain orientation and elemental composition in arched/loose regions at the tape edge.

[Experimental Design Details]
- All electrical and magnetic measurements were carried out at 77 K; no other temperatures are reported.  
- Magnetic field orientation was fixed parallel to the crystallographic c-axis (B || c).  
- No information is given on sample mounting, contact geometry, voltage-tap separation, or loop sizes for magnetic measurements.  
- Slitting-induced cracks are acknowledged but not quantified; authors argue that the observed Jc trend cannot be explained by cracking alone.

Title: Thickness-driven pinning landscape engineering in 3.3 µm EuBa2Cu3O7−δ with 6 mol% BaHfO3 for ultra-high Jc at 4.2 K and reduced angular anisotropy

Objective and Hypotheses
- Objective: Develop and validate an industrially scalable process that exploits thickness-dependent microstructure evolution in EuBa2Cu3O7−δ (EuBCO) doped with 6 mol% BaHfO3 (BHO) to create a three-dimensional (3-D) mixed pinning landscape combining highly splayed BHO nanocolumns/nanoparticles, tolerated low-angle grain boundaries, and controlled interface quality, to achieve:
  - Jc ≈ 5 MA/cm² at 4.2 K, 14 T (B parallel to c-axis) in 3.3 µm films.
  - Angular anisotropy ratio < 1.2 at 30 K, 5 T.
  - Tc ≈ 97 K with narrow transition ΔTc ≈ 0.6 K.
- Hypotheses:
  1) High-rate, multi-cycle MPMT-PLD with dynamic temperature control increases BHO nanocolumn splay (0–20°) and produces a dense mix of correlated and random pins, slowing Jc(B) decay and reducing Jc(θ) anisotropy.
  2) Accepting limited misoriented EuBCO grains nucleated on Cu–O particles introduces additional isotropic pinning without severely suppressing Tc, causing a modest reduction in self-field Jc at 77 K but improved in-field performance.
  3) A step-wise heater-temperature ramp during multi-cycle deposition preserves an optimal growth window at the bottom interface, maintaining c-axis template quality and high Tc in thick films.
  4) Intermittent thermal cycling partially relaxes growth stress, limiting microstrain increase and preventing cracking.

Experimental Design
- Overview: A factorial study on IBAD-textured templates compares baseline and modified processes to isolate the roles of (i) BHO content and morphology, (ii) misoriented grains, (iii) interface control via temperature ramp, (iv) thickness/multi-cycle stress management.

A. Sample Matrix and Controls
- Substrates and buffers: Hastelloy tape with standard buffer stack (e.g., Y2O3/YSZ/CeO2 or LaMnO3) on IBAD-MgO templates with in-plane Δφ ≈ 4–6° and out-of-plane Δω ≈ 3–5°. Tape width: 4–10 mm. Use 20–50 cm segments for development.
- Target compositions: 
  - EuBCO (stoichiometric, 1–2% excess Cu to reduce cation deficiency).
  - EuBCO + 6 mol% BHO (single composite target for production runs); optional auxiliary pure BHO target for fine adjustment in multi-plume mode.
- Sample sets (n ≥ 3 per condition for statistics):
  1) Baseline thin control: EuBCO + 6% BHO, 1.1 µm, single-cycle deposition, standard temperature (constant heater setpoint), minimal splay (benchmark).
  2) Baseline thick control: EuBCO + 6% BHO, 3.3 µm, single-cycle (no thermal breaks, no ramp), standard temperature (tests stress and texture limits).
  3) Target process: EuBCO + 6% BHO, 3.3 µm, multi-cycle (6 sub-layers ~0.55 µm each) with step-wise heater-temperature ramp and rotation/speed schedule designed to increase splay.
  4) Ablations:
     - A1 (no BHO): EuBCO, 3.3 µm, multi-cycle ramp (tests BHO necessity).
     - A2 (no ramp): EuBCO + 6% BHO, 3.3 µm, multi-cycle without heater ramp (tests interface control).
     - A3 (low splay): EuBCO + 6% BHO, 3.3 µm, multi-cycle with reduced growth rate and plume symmetry (tests splay role).
     - A4 (suppress misorientation): EuBCO + 6% BHO, 3.3 µm, process tuned to minimize Cu–O particles (tests misoriented-grain contribution).
     - A5 (single-cycle stress): EuBCO + 6% BHO, 3.3 µm, single cycle with same net fluence (tests stress relaxation).

B. Deposition Protocol (MPMT-PLD)
- System: Industrial multi-plume, multi-turn PLD (MPMT-PLD) with reel-to-reel handling; KrF excimer laser (248 nm).
- Laser and plume parameters:
  - Repetition rate: 300 Hz (per active plume); 2–4 synchronized plumes for uniform coverage.
  - Pulse energy: 700–1000 mJ; spot area 20–40 mm²; fluence 1.5–2.5 J/cm².
  - Plume-to-substrate distance: 45–60 mm; plume incidence angle adjusted to distribute particulates.
- Ambient: O2 pressure 0.8–1.0 Torr during growth; 200–400 Torr during post-growth cool-down; ex situ oxygenation as detailed below.
- Temperature control:
  - Heater setpoint 1000–1100 °C (to maintain tape surface ~780–820 °C; confirm by two-color pyrometry and embedded thermocouple calibration).
  - Multi-cycle temperature ramp: For 6 cycles to 3.3 µm, ramp heater +15–25 °C per cycle relative to previous cycle’s setpoint to compensate for view-factor and surface-cooling changes as topography evolves; adjust tape speed to maintain constant surface temperature within ±5 °C of the target growth window.
- Tape speed and rate:
  - Stationary or step-and-repeat during development; for continuous runs, linear speed 0.2–0.5 m/h equivalent to a net deposition rate 0.8–1.5 nm/s per plume, yielding ~0.55 µm per cycle in 6–12 min of net ablation.
  - Between cycles: 3–5 min dwell at growth ambient for thermal equilibration; optional short 1 min oxygen burst to 2 Torr to smooth the surface.
- Splay control:
  - Increase splay by: higher instantaneous growth rate (300 Hz, multi-plume), slight oscillations of oxygen pressure (±0.1–0.2 Torr) at cycle transitions, programmed variation of substrate rotation speed (e.g., 5–15 rpm modulation) and minor off-axis plume alignment (±5–10°) to promote meandering; reduce splay in A3 by lowering rate (≤100 Hz) and enforcing axial plume symmetry.
- Particulate/misoriented grain tuning:
  - To tolerate controlled misorientation (target condition): slightly Cu-rich target (1–2%) and brief low pO2 pre-burst (0.6 Torr for 30 s) at cycle start to allow sparse Cu–O nanoparticle nucleation that seeds isolated a-axis grains; suppress in A4 by using stoichiometric target and maintaining pO2 ≥1 Torr at cycle start with higher surface temperature for enhanced 2D layer-by-layer growth.
- Post-growth oxygenation:
  - Cool in 400 Torr O2 from growth temperature to 500 °C at 10 °C/min; ex situ anneal in flowing O2 (1 bar) at 450 °C for 60–90 min; cool to room temperature in O2 to set δ for Tc ≈ 97 K.

C. Structural and Microstructural Characterization
- X-ray diffraction (high-resolution):
  - θ–2θ scans: confirm c-axis orientation, extract c-axis lattice parameter using Nelson–Riley extrapolation (target ≈ 11.73 Å).
  - Rocking curve (ω-scan) of (005): FWHM target ≈ 1.5° across thickness.
  - φ-scan of (103): FWHM target ≈ 2°; evaluate texture uniformity at multiple positions along length.
  - Williamson–Hall plots: estimate microstrain; target increase from ~0.21% (1.1 µm) to ≤0.25% (3.3 µm).
- SEM and AFM:
  - Surface roughness per cycle (Rq target ≤ 5–8 nm); detect particulates.
- Cross-sectional TEM/STEM:
  - Lamellae at 0.3, 1.1, 2.2, 3.3 µm depths via FIB; HAADF-STEM imaging for BHO nanocolumns and nanoparticles; quantify:
    - Column diameter (3–8 nm), density (vol% 4–10%), spacing (10–20 nm), and length continuity.
    - Splay angle distribution: mean and FWHM per depth; goal: broadened 0–20° distribution in thick film vs narrow near-0° in thin control.
    - Fraction of a-axis grains and low-angle boundaries; correlate with Cu–O particle density via EDS (Hf-M, Ba-L, Eu-M, Cu-K mapping).
  - STEM-EELS/EDS: confirm Hf-rich nanocolumn composition (Ba:Hf ≈ 1:1), verify BHO-free layered regions and their thickness/spacing.
- Residual stress and integrity:
  - Cross-sectional SEM/TEM to check for cracks/voids; bend tests to 1% tensile strain to verify no catastrophic cracking.

D. Electrical and Magnetic Measurements
- Resistivity and Tc:
  - Four-probe ρ(T) in PPMS: 300–10 K at 1–5 mA; Tc onset and ΔTc (10–90% criterion); goal Tc ≈ 97 K, ΔTc ≈ 0.6 K.
- Self-field Jc at 77 K:
  - Transport on 3–5 mm wide bridges; 1 µV/cm criterion; compare targeted process vs A4 (suppressed misorientation). Accept modest reduction (e.g., 1.4 vs 2.6 MA/cm²).
- In-field magnetization Jc:
  - PPMS VSM/Magnet up to 16–18 T, 4.2 K and 30 K; extract Jc using Bean model for rectangular cross-section; measure Fp = JcB.
  - Determine Birr via Kramer plots (Jc^1/2 vs B).
- Angular transport Jc:
  - 18 T split-pair or resistive magnet with rotator; 4.2 K and 30 K; 1 µV/cm criterion; θ sweep 0–180° at fixed B: 5, 10, 14, 18 T; alignment accuracy ±0.2°; compute anisotropy ratio Γ = Jc,max/Jc,min; target Γ < 1.2 at 30 K, 5 T; measure peak broadening near H||c.

E. Data Analysis and Evaluation Criteria
- Pinning-force scaling:
  - Fit reduced field b = B/Birr; Dew-Hughes model Fp(b) ~ b^p(1−b)^q; track bmax shift (random pins bmax ≈ 0.2–0.3; correlated pins shifts and shoulder formation).
  - Compare Fp,max and Fp at 14–18 T to quantify high-field improvements.
- Anisotropic scaling:
  - Apply Blatter scaling with mass anisotropy γ (expected ~5–7 for REBCO). Quantify deviations from scaling as a measure of correlated pin dominance and splay effectiveness.
- Thickness effects:
  - Plot Jc and Fp vs thickness for 1.1, 2.2, 3.3 µm; ensure slower Jc(B) decay at 4.2 K and improved Jc(θ) isotropy with thickness in target process vs controls.
- Texture-performance linkage:
  - Correlate ω, φ FWHM and fraction of a-axis grains with self-field and in-field Jc; verify low-angle boundaries do not depress Tc or broaden ΔTc.
- Success criteria:
  - Achieve Jc ≈ 5 MA/cm² at 4.2 K, 14 T (H||c) on 3.3 µm films with Γ < 1.2 at 30 K, 5 T, Tc ≈ 97 K, ΔTc ≤ 0.6 K, ω ≈ 1.5°, φ ≈ 2°.

Ablation Study Design (Isolate Each Strategy)
- Remove BHO (A1): Expect strong drop in high-field Jc and restoration of stronger anisotropy; confirms necessity of nanocolumn/nanoparticle pins.
- Remove ramp (A2): Expect degraded Tc and broader ΔTc due to interface degradation; possible increased a-axis grains at bottom; confirms interface-temperature control.
- Reduce splay (A3): Expect pronounced c-axis peak in Jc(θ) and higher anisotropy; Fp(b) peak shifts toward lower b; confirms splay role in isotropy.
- Suppress misorientation (A4): Expect higher 77 K self-field Jc but lower high-field Jc and increased anisotropy; confirms beneficial isotropic pin contribution from tolerated misorientation.
- Single-cycle growth (A5): Expect higher microstrain (≥0.28%), possible crack initiation and slightly worse texture; confirms stress-relief role of multi-cycle deposition.

Implementation of Technologies and Methods
- MPMT-PLD Hardware and Process Control
  - Multi-plume optics: Beam splitters or multiple lasers addressing composite EuBCO+BHO targets; synchronized scanning to obtain uniform ablation and stoichiometry.
  - Temperature metrology: Two-color pyrometer aimed at tape surface; embedded thermocouple in dummy substrate for absolute calibration; closed-loop control to achieve ±5 °C stability.
  - Oxygen delivery: Fast-acting MFCs and throttling valve to program ±0.1–0.2 Torr excursions at cycle boundaries.
  - Substrate motion: Programmable rotation 5–30 rpm with sinusoidal modulation; reel-to-reel motion with pause points for cycle transitions.
  - Target management: Densified ceramic EuBCO+BHO target (>95% theoretical density) sintered 950–1000 °C; raster scanning to minimize cone formation; target conditioning 10–15 min prior to deposition.
- Growth Window Rationale
  - REBCO PLD optimal surface temperature is ~770–820 °C; industrial heater setpoints near 1000–1100 °C compensate for radiative losses and emissivity of moving tapes. The multi-cycle ramp compensates for increased radiative loss and morphology-induced view-factor changes as thickness accumulates.
- BHO Nanocolumn Formation and Splay
  - Self-assembly of perovskite BHO nanocolumns occurs by strain-driven phase separation during PLD; higher growth rate and mild off-axis plume incidence promote meandering and splay. Nanoparticle co-precipitates form when local supersaturation and growth interruptions occur at cycle boundaries, adding random point/short-range pins.
- Managing Misoriented Grains
  - Sparse Cu–O nanoparticles (few per µm²) can seed locally misoriented EuBCO grains with low-angle boundaries. By slightly Cu-rich targets and brief low pO2 at cycle begins, their density can be tuned. Boundaries act as isotropic pins when angle is small; excessive density is avoided to prevent weak-link networks.
- Interface Preservation
  - First sub-layer deposited with carefully maintained surface temperature and slightly higher pO2 to maximize epitaxy from buffer template. Subsequent layers use dynamic adjustments to preserve c-axis dominance while allowing controlled splay.
- Oxygenation Protocol
  - Thick films require thorough oxygenation; staged cool-down and ex situ anneal ensure δ optimized for high Tc while avoiding Hf oxide reduction or secondary reactions.

Feasibility Assessment
- Equipment and Resources
  - Industrial MPMT-PLD line (KrF lasers, multi-plume heads), oxygen delivery, reel-to-reel handling, XRD with rocking/phi capability, FIB and TEM/STEM with EDS/EELS, PPMS with VSM and rotator, 18 T transport magnet station, cryogenic infrastructure.
  - Materials: IBAD templates, EuBCO and BHO powders, composite targets, oxygen supply.
  - Personnel: 1 PLD process engineer, 1 materials scientist (XRD/SEM/AFM), 1 TEM specialist, 1 low-temperature transport specialist, 1 data analyst.
- Timeline (indicative)
  - Months 0–1: Target fabrication and PLD calibration (rate/temperature mapping, pyrometry).
  - Months 2–3: Make sample sets (baseline and target), initial XRD/SEM, 77 K self-field measurements.
  - Months 3–5: TEM/STEM across thickness; PPMS magnetization, 18 T transport angular studies.
  - Month 6: Ablation sets (A1–A5), analysis, model fitting, iteration if needed.
- Risks and Mitigations
  - Excess particulates or high a-axis fraction: Mitigate via plume conditioning, target resurfacing, higher pO2 at cycle start, and optimized rotation.
  - Delamination/cracking in thick films: Use multi-cycle stress relief, verify microstrain by Williamson–Hall; adjust cycle thickness if needed.
  - Oxygen deficiency in thick films: Extend ex situ anneal or add in situ high-pO2 soak; verify by Tc and ρ(T) residual resistivity ratio.
  - Hf segregation or secondary phases: Maintain growth window; verify via EDS line scans and adjust growth rate or pO2 to keep BHO coherent.
  - Reproducibility along length: Sample at leading/middle/trailing tape sections; ensure ±10% uniformity in Jc and texture metrics.

References to Previous Studies (pre-2025)
- Foltyn, J. et al., Materials science challenges for high-temperature superconducting coated conductors. Nature Materials 6, 631–642 (2007). Overview of REBCO CC growth, texture, and defects.
- MacManus-Driscoll, J. L. et al., Strongly enhanced current densities in superconducting YBa2Cu3O7−x films using BaZrO3. Applied Physics Letters 84, 5329 (2004). Nanoparticle/nanorod pinning concept groundwork.
- Gutiérrez, J. et al., Strong isotropic pinning in solution-derived YBa2Cu3O7−x nanocomposite films. Nature Materials 6, 367–373 (2007). Self-assembled secondary phases and isotropic pinning.
- Maiorov, B. et al., Synergetic combination of different types of defects to reduce anisotropy and enhance pinning in YBa2Cu3O7. Nature Materials 8, 398–404 (2009). Mixed pinning landscapes reduce angular anisotropy.
- Miura, M. et al., Strong flux pinning at low temperatures in REBCO coated conductors with Ba-based perovskite nanorods. Applied Physics Letters 96, 072514 (2010). High-field, 4.2 K pinning from nanorods.
- Selvamanickam, V. et al., Strong flux pinning in high-temperature superconducting films at 4.2 K and 31 T by BaZrO3 and BaHfO3 doping. Superconductor Science and Technology 27, 125009 (2014). BHO efficacy at low temperature, high fields.
- Mele, P. et al., Flux pinning in YBCO films with BaHfO3 nanoparticles and nanorods. Applied Physics Letters 98, 152503 (2011). BHO-specific nanostructures and pinning.
- Blatter, G. et al., Vortices in high-temperature superconductors. Reviews of Modern Physics 66, 1125–1388 (1994). Anisotropic scaling and vortex physics framework.
- Dew-Hughes, D., Flux pinning mechanisms in type II superconductors. Philosophical Magazine 30, 293–305 (1974). Pinning-force scaling model.
- Bean, C. P., Magnetization of high-field superconductors. Reviews of Modern Physics 36, 31–39 (1964). Bean critical state model.
- Williamson, G. K. & Hall, W. H., X-ray line broadening from filed aluminium and tungsten. Acta Metallurgica 1, 22–31 (1953). Microstrain analysis.
- Nelson, J. B. & Riley, D. P., An experimental investigation of extrapolation methods in the derivation of accurate unit-cell dimensions of crystals. Proceedings of the Physical Society 57, 160 (1945). Nelson–Riley method.
- Iijima, Y. et al., Biaxially aligned YBa2Cu3O7−x films on polycrystalline metal substrates by IBAD and PLD. Physica C 335, 107–111 (2000). IBAD-PLD coated conductor methodology.
- Wee, S. H. et al., Self-assembled nanostructure engineering in REBCO for isotropic pinning. Applied Physics Letters 102, 232603 (2013). Process–nanostructure control and isotropy.

Clarity Notes (key terms)
- c-axis and a-axis grains: EuBCO has layered crystal structure; c-axis perpendicular to tape; a-axis grains are misoriented and can create weaker links if excessive.
- Splayed nanocolumns: Columnar BHO defects tilted at various angles; they act as correlated pinning sites and broaden the angular range of strong pinning.
- Bean model: Converts magnetic hysteresis into Jc by assuming a critical state current distribution.
- Dew-Hughes scaling: Empirical model to categorize dominant pinning mechanisms from Fp(b) behavior.
- Anisotropic scaling (Blatter): Rescales field by effective mass anisotropy to test whether pinning is dominated by random, uncorrelated defects; deviations indicate correlated pinning.

Step-by-Step Summary
Step 1: Calibrate MPMT-PLD growth window (surface temperature vs heater setpoint; deposition rate vs laser parameters; oxygen transients).
Step 2: Fabricate baseline 1.1 µm and 3.3 µm films (single-cycle and multi-cycle), plus ablation sets A1–A5.
Step 3: Execute multi-cycle process with per-cycle heater ramp and programmed splay-promoting parameters (rate, rotation, pO2 modulation).
Step 4: Oxygenate and cool using staged protocol; dice test bridges.
Step 5: Perform XRD (θ–2θ, ω, φ), extract c-axis (Nelson–Riley), microstrain (Williamson–Hall).
Step 6: TEM/STEM-EDS across thickness to quantify nanocolumn density, splay distribution, nanoparticle population, a-axis fraction, Cu–O seeds.
Step 7: Measure ρ(T), Tc, and ΔTc; 77 K self-field Jc; PPMS magnetization Jc(B) at 4.2 K and 30 K; extract Fp(b), Birr.
Step 8: Transport Jc(θ) at 4.2 K and 30 K in 5–18 T; compute anisotropy ratio and compare with Blatter scaling predictions.
Step 9: Analyze ablation results to attribute performance gains to BHO content/morphology, splay, interface control, and misorientation; confirm stress relief via microstrain and integrity checks.
Step 10: Iterate process parameters if needed to meet targets; document process windows compatible with meter-scale production.

Criteria for Validation
- Structural: ω ≤ 1.6°, φ ≤ 2.2°, c ≈ 11.73 Å stable; microstrain ≤ 0.25% at 3.3 µm; absence of cracks.
- Electrical: Tc ≈ 97 K, ΔTc ≤ 0.6 K; Jc(4.2 K, 14 T, H||c) ≈ 5 MA/cm²; Γ(30 K, 5 T) < 1.2.
- Causality: Ablation studies show expected directional changes in Jc(B,θ), Fp(b), and Tc/ΔTc, confirming each strategy’s role.
